utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Today, we are Thursday, the 22nd of May, 2008. I would like to greet the witness, the Prosecutor, Mr. Seselj, Mr. Seselj's associates, who honour us with their presence today. I would also like to greet all the people assisting us in the courtroom today. We need to resume the testimony of our witness this morning. He is an expert witness. We have a map here in the courtroom. The examination-in-chief is about to begin, but before that, Mr. Mundis, a housekeeping matter, to avoid having to address it at a quarter past 1.00, at the end of the hearing. Next week, what is your schedule? Rather, your schedule is as follows: There shall be Witness 051 next week. He is a protected witness. I will not give his name. We will start off our hearing next week with Witness 051, as planned. Next week, we shall be sitting in the afternoon, so we will have our next hearing next Tuesday at a quarter to 2:00 with Witness 051. Is that right, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe we had the other perhaps hearing scheduled first on Tuesday of next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, 051 has been officially scheduled. If there's another hearing, we shall see what needs to be done when the time comes. We shall meet again on Tuesday in the presence of Witness 051, next Tuesday in this courtroom, at a quarter to 2:00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is certainly the plan, Mr. President. Again, hopefully we'll be able to finish Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony today, in which case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the condition that we do finish today. Without wasting any more time, I will give you the floor now, Mr. Mundis -- Mr. Seselj. I said in order not to waste any time. I hope that we shall save time, rather than the contrary.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't want to waste time either, Mr. President, although yesterday, for two and a half hours, I was kept here in the cell and only then transported to the prison. And this morning, I was picked up at 7.15. That's just, for your information, to illustrate the situation. Before the examination-in-chief, I would like the Prosecutor now to specify what the real title of the expert report of Mr. Riedlmayer is, word by word, so that we know the real heading, because in this heap of documents that I've received, and matters are quite contradictory there, we have various titles, so I'd like to hear the proper one, the real one. The last one says: "The destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina," for example. Is it that latest title that holds true or do the previous titles apply? So what is the exact title of the expert report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, what is the definitive title?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the definitive title of the report, which bears 65 ter number 00463 is: "Destruction of Cultural Heritage in Bosnia-Herzegovina." It is subtitled: "A Post-War Survey of the Destruction of Non Serb Cultural Heritage in the Municipalities of Bijeljina, Bosansk Samac, Brcko, Mostar, Nevesinje, Greater Sarajevo, Ilidza, Ilijas, Novi Grad, Rajlovac, Novo Sarajevo, Vogusca and Zvornik during the 1992-1995 War, with Specific Reference to the Period September 1991 to September 1993." It is indeed the one in the binder which the Presiding Judge has, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is, Mr. Seselj. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and let me start by saying good morning to the Trial Chamber, Dr. Seselj, his associates, and to Mr. Riedlmayer, as well as everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, could you please tell the Trial Chamber about your educational background?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm a native of Hungary. I was educated in West Germany and the United States. I attended the University of Chicago, where I have an undergraduate degree, in history, bachelor's degree. I have a master's degree from Princeton University in Near Eastern Studies, and I have a Master's degree in Library and Information Science from Simmons College.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Riedlmayer, you briefly told us yesterday where you're currently employed. Can you just give us a little bit of your professional background following your education?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since 1985, I have been employed as bibliographer in Islamic art and architecture, directing the Documentation Centre for Islamic Art and Architecture of the Aga Khan programme at Harvard University. This is probably the largest documentation centre on the subject of Islamic art and architecture in North America and one of the largest in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, within this field of Islamic art and architecture, what, if any, special expertise do you hold?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My special expertise is in the methods of documentation and the kinds of material that we acquire, catalogue, make available to researchers and use in our own research, which ranges from published information to unpublished photographs, architectural drawings, and ephemera. In addition, I have a long record of publications which is listed in my curriculum vitae in professional and academic journals, concentrating largely but not exclusively on the history, art and architecture of the Ottoman period in the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, what research or work you've done with respect to cultural property during periods of war in the Balkans?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For roughly the past decade and a half, I have been researching the destruction of cultural property in the Balkan wars. I have done so both in terms of academic research and field research. I have done extensive fieldwork after the conflict, both in Kosovo and in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit, Mr. Riedlmayer, about this, as you've put it, extensive fieldwork? What did that entail, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fieldwork entailed going into these areas in the aftermath of conflict, visiting sites concerning which there had been allegations of destruction, documenting what I found at those sites, collecting documentation from sources deemed to be reliable, compiling this documentation and making conclusions about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And yesterday, in response to some preliminary questions from the Presiding Judge, you told us that you had testified on a number of occasions. Can you very quickly again indicate which cases you have testified in?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've testified about the destruction of cultural property in Kosovo in the Milosevic-Kosovo and the Milutinovic et al case here at the ICTY. I've testified about the destruction of cultural property in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the Milosevic-Bosnia case, in the Krajisnik case, in the lawsuit brought before the International Court of Justice by Bosnia-Herzegovina concerning the application of the Convention on Genocide, and now in the current case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Riedlmayer, when you make reference to cultural property, can you please give us a succinct definition of what you mean?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Cultural property," in this sense, is the cultural heritage of nations. It consists primarily in the areas studied of houses of worship, historic architecture, and libraries and archives and museums.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn, sir, to the specific task that you were given with respect to this case. Can you tell us what it is that you were asked to do with respect to the report that was produced in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the report in this case, I was asked to prepare a report, and supporting documentation, on the destruction of non-Serb, that is, Muslim and Catholic Croat, cultural property in a specified set of municipalities. This included a subset of the municipalities that were included in my report for the Milosevic and Krajisnik cases, plus certain additional municipalities that were included in this indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you tell us, please, what material you produced as part of the task you were given in this case?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: For this case, I produced, first of all, a database of 158 entries, one entry for each site documented, as well as a summary report of roughly 30 pages, which you have before you. In addition, there were other supplementary materials that were submitted as appendices to that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I'd like to draw your attention, sir, to one of those appendices in particular. That concerns what I believe is described as a database. Can you tell us a little bit about this database?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The database is simply a useful way of tabulating information about specific sites. It allows one to gather together, first of all, photographs. When available, I always try to include a variety of photographs, before and after shots of a building from different angles and so forth. Secondly, it allows one to take textural information that relates to specific questions, such as location, condition, and other information about the building, and put it into fields where one can tabulate it across the database, so one can easily, with the help of the database, pull up answers to questions such as: How many of the monuments that were damaged had been legally-protected monuments? How many monuments were undamaged or severely damaged? How many monuments were in a given municipality? So that is what a database is. I believe every entry from the database has been printed out, and each database entry was formatted to three A4 pages. Now, obviously not the same amount of documentation was available for every site, so in some cases the printed pages are blank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And those printed pages are one of the attachments, if you will, to your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that database, was it primarily designed to be a printed document or was it something that was to be used electronically?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was primarily designed to be used electronically.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you again just tell us why it is that the database was designed to be used electronically?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply because it's not easy to navigate across 158 sites, and more importantly, these ways of sorting it that I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Riedlmayer, I understand, from the time you spent with one of my colleagues over the past few days, that you produced or assisted in the production of a slide show, a Powerpoint slide show. Can you tell us a little bit about that, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. With the exception of a couple of maps --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. That kind of leading question is impermissible. We're not interested in what Mr. Mundis understood from certain earlier conversations. He must ask a direct question. And we're not interested in the proofing session of his colleague with the expert witness, either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you were just explaining why you had this map; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Not the large map, Your Honours, but we do have a Powerpoint presentation that's based on the report. That would be a useful aid for the Trial Chamber in terms of navigating the expert's report and the attachments, and I simply wanted him to explain, before we move to that demonstrative aid, how that was produced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. [No interpretation] Let me repeat. If I have understood you correctly, this Powerpoint slide show was prepared in order to facilitate your work and the work of the expert. This was addressed during the proofing session, and this is what you're trying to tell us so that we better understand how this works; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, let me try to explain what it is we would like to do, and then perhaps the witness can explain a little bit more about this Powerpoint presentation. What we've done is taken the expert report and the hundreds of pages of annexes and put it into a format that makes the presentation of that evidence easier to comprehend in a short period of time, highlighting, for example, conclusions, highlighting certain examples, so that we don't have a situation where we're trying to go through 800 pages of a printout of an electronic database here in court. It's simply a way to expedite this. This presentation that we would like to show, I would like to ask the witness how it was created and then proceed by way of using this Powerpoint presentation to bring out the salient points, if you will, from the expert's report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who has prepared it; did you or did the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That was precisely the question I was trying to ask the witness when the objection arose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you explain, Mr. Riedlmayer, how this Powerpoint [French spoken] was produced?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Powerpoint presentation is simply a slide show. For the purposes of this Powerpoint, I took the images from the database and selected images that would illustrate conclusions and certain points in the report, and I worked with the Office of the Prosecutor to structure it in such a way that it reflected the report. The only material shown in the Powerpoint that is not in the database are three or four maps that were included at the beginning just to orient the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, with that explanation, we would now like to move into this Powerpoint presentation as a way of expediting and efficiently presenting this material to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already said that I object, and wanted to object again before Mr. Mundis asked this question, Mr. President. I don't know if you'd noticed that I'd raised my hand to object. Quite obviously from all this, they prepared this presentation together, that is to say, the expert witness and the Prosecution, and not the expert witness himself alone, independently, because once he signed a contract and agreement with the Prosecutor, it was up to him to prepare his testimony in court independently. Of course, he could have had preparatory discussions, but to have prepared the presentation together, I don't think that has been seen in The Hague -- even in The Hague Tribunal before. And nobody's explained to me what "Powerpoint" is, in fact. It should have been explained to me previously, and if we're going to have some accelerated presentation here, then I demand far more time for the cross-examination than the Prosecutor was given for the in-chief, because I have no Powerpoint and I have to ask questions about each and every detail. And I am challenging a great deal from this expert witness's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Expert, we have two problems here. We have a problem of a technical nature. Since we don't know what it is, nobody can challenge anything whatsoever, because we don't know what this is about. But there is another problem which the accused has just raised and which is more important. You're an expert witness, and therefore, per se, you are impartial. It's not because the Prosecutor has asked you to come that you depend on the OTP. When you prepared this Powerpoint slide show, did you do it independently or did the Prosecutor tell you, "You need to do this, you need to do that," and so on and so forth, or, in light of the subject matter, you said, "This is how things should be done"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecutor provided primarily technical assistance. All the material in the Powerpoint, Powerpoint being, as a matter of explanation simply a presentation software that allows one to project slides on a computer, it is in effect no different than using photographic slides, only one can do it by computer. But all the material in the Powerpoint presentation, it's all photographs, and the photographs all come from my database. So this is not something that was created out of new material, and the structure of it arises out of my report. It is not something that was dictated to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This software is a software which is off the shelf; it's not something which the Prosecution set up? It's a software package that anybody can get hold of; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is one of the most common softwares used in business presentations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, if you want to show your holiday photographs, you can also use this software, is that right, if you want to view your holiday photographs? You can. Well, we'll have a look at it. If there are objects to the effect that the Prosecutor is behind all of this, we shall notice it pretty quickly, but first of all let's see the upside rather than the downside first. Mr. Mundis, let's start viewing this, because we are talking about something which I find difficult to understand. But as soon as we have the pictures on the screen, we will understand better, won't we? And if Mr. Seselj then feels that the rights of the accused have been violated, he will let us know. But for the time being, I don't know, so let's begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We do have handouts of these Powerpoint slides that were produced and distributed to Dr. Seselj yesterday. I do have I believe extra copies here that may be helpful either now or at the conclusion of the presentation. I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands, but we do have sufficient copies for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Everything that I was disclosed and perhaps represents a Powerpoint is in my cell because it's exclusively in English. What I received is this [indicates] in Serbian, one binder. It's quite thin, as well, and in English two much longer binders, perhaps twice as much as this, so four times the amount of material. But as I say, anything in English, I cannot use. I see that there are colour photographs there and whatever else, but what do photographs in English mean to me? Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I understood what you said, Mr. Mundis. On the screen, we see one photograph which represents Bosnia-Herzegovina. We see the names of the countries, which are in English. Perhaps Mr. Seselj would like all of this to be translated into Serbian. Maybe that is not required that Belarus be translated into Serbian, or Poland or Germany, be translated into Serbian, unless he doesn't know his geography so well. So I don't think that's a problem. As far as the photographs are concerned, are there any captions in English, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, all the photographs are captioned both in English and in B/C/S, in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that settles the issue. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I should also note for the record that this slide show is in e-court, and it bears 65 ter number 00463A. If we could then turn to the slide, Mr. Riedlmayer, that you see on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what the purpose of this slide was, please?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of the first three slides is just brief geographic orientation as to which areas I covered in my survey. So we can go to the next slide. Obviously, the blue-outlined area is Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these are the municipalities that are related to the indictment. And the next slide. And these are the municipalities that were covered in my report. If you count the municipalities, you should take account of the fact that what's labelled "Sarajevo" is actually Greater Sarajevo, which is five municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, before we move further, sir, can you just tell us a little about --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, the witness has assisted us a lot now. I think that the Prosecutor should first state to the Trial Chamber why the expert report does not include all the localities that are covered by the indictment, or perhaps the Prosecutor has another expert in store that would deal with other localities and we don't know about this expert because he's not on the list, he hasn't been announced. Why is a selection of localities listed in the indictment done? The Prosecutor has failed to explain that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, could you answer? According to Mr. Seselj -- I haven't counted everything, but it seems that there are localities which were omitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, these are all issues that could be raised, first of all, during cross-examination, but I can ask the witness why he was tasked with looking at these 11 municipalities. That would certainly be something that the witness could answer. The larger issues as to why or how the Prosecution structured its case are not issues that we need to go into at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the question raised is a question that I had asked myself earlier on, and I wanted to ask it right away. I did not, and maybe I should have. In your report, I noted that there were 11 municipalities. It starts with Bijeljina, Bosansk Samac, and Nevesinje and Zvornik. Then I noted -- I wondered whether Vukovar was included, since Vukovar was part of the indictment, but it is not included in your report, so I thought about this. We have had witnesses here who came and testified and gave us their version of the events which, after all, were a bit different from what you could have thought from reading the indictment. In Vukovar, as an example, we noted through witnesses that before the JNA entered Vukovar, there had been conflicts, conflicts against the Croats and the Serbs. Given this, if even before the JNA enters there is already a conflict, one can already justly wonder whether Croats -- well, this is just, you know, an assumption -- whether Croats wouldn't have destroyed Orthodox churches. That's the first question that one could put. And then I'll come to Zvornik, because you have also studied Zvornik. Well, through witnesses, we've noted -- we've found out that in Zvornik there had been incidents before large-scale operation were carried out, incidents had occurred. This is what the evidence seems to indicate. So if there are incidents, one could really go through the following logic: There is incidents pitting community A against community B, so community A is going to destroy property belonging to community B. And after a while, people from community B will destroy properties from community A. But in the first step, you know, when the As destroy property from the Bs, if this does not appear in the expert report, this could lead to misunderstandings. And with this in mind, when I studied your report, I noted it said the following: You took photographs of churches and mosques that had been destroyed, but I really wondered why you had not destroyed [as interpreted] the orthodox churches that could have been destroyed in exactly the same picture --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, I really wonder why you had not have taken pictures of the Orthodox churches that could have been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I was wondering why you decided to select a number of cities and why, in your report, you did not also take pictures of Orthodox churches which may have been destroyed maybe before, during or after the event, so that we would have the entire picture of what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not set the terms of the mission. When I was first approached to produce a report, they asked whether I would be prepared to do one for the Croatian municipalities as well, such as Vocin or Vukovar. However, I informed the Office of the Prosecutor that I had done no fieldwork in Croatia, and so they decided that I should limit it to Bosnia, where I had done fieldwork. As to the decision not to include Serb heritage in the survey, that again was not mine. Due to limitations of time, the total amount of time I had available for the most systematic fieldwork that I did was slightly under a month, and in that survey I covered more than 4.000 kilometres and worked very long days. And so in order to cover the maximum amount of territory, it was decided by the Office of the Prosecutor to make the assignment the destruction of non-Serb cultural property. However, I should say that I made observations and, indeed, took some photographs of the Orthodox churches that I encountered that had suffered damage in the war, and so I'm aware of them. And in another report that I did for this Tribunal for Kosovo, I did cover the Serb property, so the decision not to include it in this report was not my choice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We understood you well. You told us that you were on the field, you went to Bosnia-Herzegovina. I myself went there also, and it's true that once you're there, you're really struck in a number of cities or localities of the number of religious buildings belonging to different religions. This is really striking when you're a foreigner. Now, if an expert comes and is interested only in the destruction of Catholic churches, when the mosque is also destroyed or the Orthodox church is also destroyed, it only takes a picture of the destroyed Catholic Church, without taking pictures of the other churches or mosques, do you belive this is a correct way of working, independently of the fact that you were commissioned only to do this? I would like to know whether, as a scientist, you should not tell the person commissioning the work that it might be too limitative [as interpreted] to only take pictures of a Catholic Church when next to it there is a destroyed mosque or destroyed orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I noted all my observations, and when examples come up, I'm willing to answer about those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I tried to shed some light on this. You can continue. Mr. Seselj, I belive I have taken stock of the problem. I don't see what you may add. Well, go ahead, it might be interesting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it is interesting to note, Mr. President, what kind of a lawyer would I be if you were able to anticipate every objection that I might make? That would make me a despicable lawyer, and that's not what I am. You can see that I was completely right when I asked that this explanation be made by the Prosecution and not the witness. Why the Prosecution did not tell the witness to deal with all the cultural heritage and monuments that have been destroyed? Secondly, if the expert was tasked with dealing with all the religious monuments and cultural heritage in Kosovo, Serbs and Albanian, that is, mostly Muslim, because most of the cultural heritage belongs to Albanians, if he dealt with that report, although we're not going to deal with that report, although I received the report fro Kosovo and Metohija then why the same methodology was not supplied here in the indictment against me. Why one methodology for the Kosovo indictment against Milosevic and the indictment against Milutinovic et al, and why another methodology for the indictment against me, Krajisnik and Milosevic in the Bosnia case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have told us on many occasions that you have chosen your own Defence strategy, so why couldn't the Prosecutor also choose his own Defence strategy, so why couldn't the Prosecutor also choose his own prosecution strategy?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have to respond, Madame Judge, if you allow me. I have to know about the strategy of the Prosecution. That's why I received the indictment, the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution. That's why I received all the evidence gathered by the Prosecution. I suppose that I got that. I hope. That's what I was supposed to, because I have to be aware of the Prosecution's strategy, and I think that you will admit that the Prosecution's strategy is not clear to you and your colleagues, because they announced they would be calling experts -- an expert for just one segment of the charges against me, and they did not call any experts for other segments. I'll tell you why. Because in Croatia, more Serb Orthodox religion buildings were torn down than Catholic ones. Unfortunately, in Bosnia, the situation is different. There was more destruction to Bosnia religious buildings than the Serb ones, but you should not neglect the Serb building, because it was a civil war with a pronounced religious component. And these are not questions for the cross-examination of the witness. The witness stated his position, and it is not his fault. He was given a task as an expert. It is the fault of the Prosecution. It's a procedural objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you will call an expert that will tell us about the Serb cultural property destroyed. Just do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, what you have just said is highlighting the procedural questions that are enforced in this Tribunal. If the Pre-Trial Judge or the Judge had appointed the expert, then this Judge would have taken into account all the elements that you have told us and we would not have this debate now that is wasting so much time, because an expert commissioned by a Judge would have taken into account all the different aspects, and this expert would have been completely independent from the parties. Unfortunately, this is not the procedure enforced in this Tribunal, with its 1994 rules. It is another kind of procedure that is in force. In this procedure, the Prosecutor can choose his own expert, commission him, give him an assignment, with everything you have just told us. But as my colleague just told you, justly, you are also entitled to call your own expert who can highlight the fact that in Croatia, there was a great number of Serbian buildings, religious buildings, who were destroyed. When the Prosecutor, through his own expert, is going to highlight a number of elements which could lead one to believe, according to what you're saying, that it is only the Catholic or Muslim buildings that were destroyed. We are under a common-law procedure. The Prosecutor has his own experts, and you will call your expert, and this is why we have, after that, an adversarial debate. Of course, you are protesting very well, it's very clever. It is wasting time, but you could have done this during the cross-examination or during the presentation of your Defence case with your own expert, because you can call your own experts, of course, and this expert can demonstrate what you are now telling us through your objection. This is how it's supposed to work here. Of course, I understood what you had thought, which is why I asked the question about the expert. Maybe I was a little bit anticipating your own words, and this is why I asked the expert why he did not ask the person commissioning him to have an extension of his assignment, and the answer was, "Well, I was asked to do a specific assignment and this is what I did." That's the way things work. Now, you raised another problem. I was not a member -- I was not on the Bench in the Milosevic or the Krajisnik trials, where you told us that the Prosecution had a different strategy. Very well, you can tell us about this during your own Defence case. We took due note of what you have said, everything is now on the transcript, but we would like to move on, move forward, keeping in mind the observations that you have said. Mr. Mundis, could you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you don't allow me to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you want to reply, please do so, but I think I've been -- I've said everything. What do you want to add, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, you said yourself that I stated that this witness had applied a different methodology for Kosovo, and I have to tell you this is not correct. That's what the first witness here said, and that was what prompted me to object. I am not going to be calling an expert to explain to us here in the courtroom why Mr. Riedlmayer used a different methodology in Kosovo and why he was given this task by the Prosecution. The witness -- or the Prosecution has to explain to you why different methodologies were applied and why this witness was given such a limited brief. What is the essence of it, what is behind it? And this is not something that my experts should explain. I am really quite flabbergasted that you are willing to overlook this major procedural error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, the issue is actually quite simple. Dr. Seselj is not charged with the destruction of orthodox, religious or cultural facilities. If we had evidence that he was involved in destroying Serbian orthodox religious or cultural facilities, we would have charged him with that and our expert would have examined that. The fact of the matter is the expert was tasked with producing a report which relates directly to the charges in the indictment against this accused. That's what the issue is all about, with all due respect, and that explains why this methodology was used; because the focus of this case is on destruction of religious or cultural property in the context of the indictment against this accused, and that cultural and religious property in this case, with respect to this accused, relates to Catholic and Islamic cultural property. That's the simplest explanation that I can give. If we had evidence that Dr. Seselj was involved in destruction of orthodox cultural property, we would have charged him with that, and Mr. Riedlmayer would have been asked to examine that as well. Let us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed. You answered -- you replied to Mr. Seselj. Very well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, would you please, in a nutshell, tell us about the process by which damage assessment was conducted with respect to your report?

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my -- in all of the reports I've done for this Tribunal, I have used a five-point assessment scale in order to be able to say something standardised about, say, a monument like the one you see on the screen to the right. It is a mosque near Bijeljina, in a village called Atmacici, and it falls into the most serious damage level. But let me please review the damage levels and explain what the criteria were for each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, in order to prevent objections, when there is an image with the title written in English, please read the title also so that the interpreters can translate for Mr. Seselj what is written on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is written on the screen is: "Damaged assessed on a five-level scale," and unfortunately, for technical reasons which I don't understand, the caption under the mosque could not be printed, but it is "Dzamija u Ahmadzici," "The mosque at Atmacici, near Bijeljina." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could, Mr. Riedlmayer, just tell us what these five levels are and how they are defined or characterized.

utterances.speaker: ANDRAS RIEDLMAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. The first level is "in good condition," which would have been applied to any building that shows no sign of war damage or of recent reconstruction. And in the municipalities surveyed for this report, I didn't find any monuments that fit that category, any religious monument. Okay. "Lightly damaged" was the least-severe damage category. It covers any damage that does not visibly compromise the main structure of the building. The damage can range from vandalism or small fires set in the building to bullet holes in the walls, which you see on this picture here, or sometimes fires in the building, even shell holes in the walls or the roof. As long as the principal part of the building appears to have survived structurally intact. This is a Catholic church in the town of Brcko. You can see that a large projectile has made an impact next to the door. There are some bullet holes. I went to the interior and it had been vandalised, all the saint's statues had their hands chopped off, but the building was clearly structurally still sound. So that is an example of a lightly-damaged building. Okay. This is a heavily-damaged building in a village near Brcko called Gorice. When I went there, I found, first of all, that the steeple was gone. It was a 35-metre-tall steeple. The apse and the alter area had collapsed and the roof was gone. Only three of the perimeter walls were still standing. When I talked to an informant, a gentleman living in the house next-door who had witnessed the attach, he said that the damage had been caused by a missile fired from a JNA aeroplane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you just describe for us, sir, because we do see on this slide two photographs, can you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. This is the first time we're hearing this. This church, you say that a neighbour told you that he saw a missile being shot from a JNA plane, so an air attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And just for the transcript, on the left, there is a shot taken in the 1980s, before the war. On the right is a photograph I took in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps go to the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, this is allegedly an expert for the destruction of cultural heritage, but here he says that he talked to a man, and that this man told him that the church had been destroyed by missiles fired from the air. What does that sound to you Judges? He was told by this man. He is an expert. Was an inquiry -- an investigation carried out? Was there a forensic expert who determined that this was destroyed from the air? I'm just making procedural objections as to why this source is used here. This man told me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These are all issues that can be raised in cross-examination, Mr. President. I would just ask that we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is another example of a heavily-damaged building. It is in the town of Mostar. It's the mosque of Sevri Hadzi Hasan, built in 1620 and a registered monument. In the slide to the right, and to orient the Court, please observe that on the intact picture, the one on the left, the darkened wall, the one next to the minaret, that is the wall that we're looking at in the "after" picture. The "after" picture is 90 degrees turned to the Left. So on the left-hand side of the picture, you see the shattered base of the minaret --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving interpretation. I haven't received any interpretation since the witness started answering the question. I haven't touched anything. Yes, I am receiving interpretation now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, could you please repeat what you said, because Mr. Seselj had not received the interpretation for the rest of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here you see before-and-after photographs of the Mosque of Sevri Hadzi Hasan in Mostar. It is one of the protected monuments in Mostar. If you take a look at careful look at the "before" shot, you see on the left-hand side of the mosque and next to the minaret, that facade is the one you see in the "after" photo. The "after" photo was taken in the summer of 1992. It is a published photograph, so I know the timing. And what you see on that photograph is the shattered base of the minaret at left, and you can see that the minaret, when it was decapitated or severed at the base, fell into the mosque, and the mosque is heavily damaged. The roof is smashed, the interior is totally wrecked, and parts of the perimeter wall are gone. Next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, the right-hand picture, when was it taken, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was taken in the summer of 1992. It comes from a documentary book prepared by the Association of Architects of Mostar, "Drustvo Arhitekata Mostar," and published in 1992. The photograph showing the destruction from the first siege of Mostar from April to June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The photograph on the right-hand side -- we have two photographers here, one on the left-hand side where we see the minaret, and the one on the right-hand side, where it's destroyed. The right-hand picture, this was taken when, in the summer of ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you this question because there was fighting in Mostar that pitched the Serbs against the Croats and the Muslims, and then there was fighting between the Muslims and the Croats. So when something is destroyed, it's important to know which period we're talking about. So you have just said that this photograph taken on the right-hand side was taken in the summer of 1992. Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in the subtitle of this report, it says that it comprises the period from 1992 to 1995, with specific reference to the period from 1991 to 1993. Now we've seen two buildings, and the witness failed to give us the date when these buildings were destroyed. And, secondly, well, I don't have the possibility of using this Powerpoint of yours in the cross-examination, no possibility to do that at all, and I have to draw your attention to the fact that these are not the same buildings. Look at the type of wall or fence around -- or the fence around the destroyed buildings and the wall around the other one, and take a look at what the building that looks like which is intact and the other one. Now, there's never a minaret built in front of the main entrance to the mosque, so I don't know how that slipped your attention. I don't have the technological possibilities of using the same Powerpoint facilities that the other side does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Expert, are you quite sure that the right-hand photograph coincides with this mosque that was built in 1620? I didn't need Mr. Seselj to tell me, because I could see this. I was looking at the wall surrounding the mosque, and on the left-hand side there is no fence. Perhaps it's difficult to see. Are you positive about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am positive. The "before" picture was taken quite some period before the war, at the beginning of the 1980s. If I consult the printout, I can probably find the exact date. And in the 1980s, there was extensive restoration of the old town, and the fence was replaced. With regards to minarets, the minaret which is the equivalent functionally of the steeple of the Christian church, in almost all mosques in Bosnia is to the right of the entrance. This was also to the right of the entrance. What you see are the windows on the side of the mosque there that is darkened. The windows that are in the "before" shot are facing the viewer or have a different pattern because they are on the so-called "mihrab" wall, that is, the sanctuary wall, the direction of prayer pointing towards mecca, and they have a little lattice screens. But I'm absolutely certain it is the same mosque, and in fact I visited it in 2002. With respect to your question, Your Honour, about the two sieges of Mostar, the one in April through June of 1992 by JNA and Serb forces and the second one in 1993-1994 by Croat forces, I was very much aware of the difficulty of sorting out damage from the two sieges, and therefore I made very sure, unlike in all of the other municipalities, although I'm very familiar with Mostar, I only used securely-dated photographs taken before the beginning of the second siege. In addition, I had the advantage that a UNESCO and Council of Europe mission, headed by Dr. Colin Kaiser, who is now the UNESCO representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, went to Mostar at the end of 1992 and did a very detailed survey of the damage, and this is cited in the entries in my database.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an ancillary question. You were an expert and you testified before the International Court, the ICJ. Who had asked you to come to testify? Was it the ICJ or was it one of the parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was one of the parties, it was Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe they have [indiscernible] expert witnesses and the agent for Serbia-Montenegro had a slightly larger number. The Court did not call any witnesses of its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Serbia and Montenegro also called witnesses to discuss those buildings that had been damaged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They called them on other matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that the witness said that in front of -- that the minaret's on the right-hand side, and you see that this destruction is on the left-hand side. The right [indiscernible] is intact, and you see the central entrance to this building and that's where the rubble is. Maybe it is a destroyed mosque, but obviously not the same one. And when cultural monuments are restored, they must be identical, the same as they were before. Now, if you look at the mosque on the left-hand side, the "before" mosque, it's in a very good state, and nobody would have the right to do away with the original stonewall that you can see there and place a metal railing here. This metal railing wasn't usual in the 17th century. You would have a stone wall in the 17th century. So where would they have had wrought iron in such large quantities to be able to use wrought iron for a railing in Herzegovina in the 17th century? Obviously, this is not the same thing, but if you are going to tolerate that, what can I do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your language is extremely concise, like the French language. You're using words which I cannot accept. This trial is broadcast to the outside world. When you are using words which are offending, I say so. No, I do not tolerate anything. This is word you used, you said "tolerate." The Prosecution is putting a question, and the Prosecution witness then answers, and you challenge this. All of this is on the transcript. We put our questions, but we do not tolerate. It's not because we don't ask any questions or that we do ask a question, that we agree either with the Prosecutor or with you. It's ultimately that we will determine whether what is being said is true or false, so don't say, "You tolerate." We don't tolerate anything at this stage. We are listening to what the Prosecution is saying, we are listening to what you are saying. Well, it's tolerative [as interpreted] to listen to both you, I tolerate that you express yourself, if you like. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, as indeed the accused was a bit confused, so was I, and my question, and I believe this is probably the same question which the accused had, is the following: What you see on the right picture, is that the main entrance of the mosque, because if so, then that would contradict your earlier statement that the main entrance was to the left of the tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not the main entrance, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can you explain what it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. It is what would be the right-hand wall of the mosque, if you were standing at the main entrance, the main entrance generally is on the front. That points towards Mecca, and the minaret is to the right of it. I only know of one exception, among several hundred mosques in Bosnia that I have seen, that was in Foca, where for various technical reasons they placed it in another spot. But that was traditional. And if you look at the "after" picture, I know it's very difficult to see with all the destruction, but you can see that without a doubt the minaret is bulging out on the left side, that that is the base of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I venture a guess, because I have not -- I did not go see that mosque before it was destroyed, but I venture a guess that what you see behind the pile of rubble, which is the remains of the minaret, is either a smashed window of the sort that you see to the right of it or a side entrance, of which there are other examples, that leads into the mosque and up the minaret or up into the women's balcony. But it is not the main entrance. The main entrance to the mosques are usually quite monumental.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if the picture could have been expanded further to the left, one would see the remnants of the main entrance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you were to look at the "after" picture and take another 90-degree turn to the left, you would see the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could now go to the next slide, and if you can tell us, sir, what the next category is. And explain the characteristics of that category.

The next category of damage is: "Heavily damaged." Heavily damaged building, according to this category, is one that has suffered significant structural damage to its main elements. Typically, this would be used to describe a building that has been completely burned out or the roof has collapsed from other causes. Often with extensive blast damage or a combination of severe damage to several parts of the structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just briefly interrupt you, Mr. Riedlmayer. On page 15, line 2, the answer was: "The next category is 'Heavily damaged'," and you went on to describe the characteristics of heavily damaged. We're now looking at a slide that says, "Almost destroyed."

I'm sorry, I lost track. Heavily damaged is several principle parts of the building such as the perimeter walls are missing or severely compromised. The building appears to be beyond repair and would require complete reconstruction, but still has some identifiable elements standing. The example here is the Franciscan Priory Church of St. Peter in Mostar. You see a pre-war photo at left from a published photo book from the 1980s. The church is visible on the left-hand side of the picture, next to a large building. That's the Franciscan monastery. The "after" photo was taken in 1992, and if you look at it, you can see, first of all, that the roof and parts of the walls have collapsed. I also have the technical report from Dr. Colin Kaiser, whom I mentioned before, who mentions that there are large fissures in the wall and that the steeple is in danger of collapsing. So this is a much more severely-damaged monument than the ones in the previous category.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can look at another example, going to the next slide, pleases.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, twice already the witness has stated that the photographs of the destroyed buildings date back to 1992, and in 1992 he did not write his expert report, so he has to prove and show that they are, indeed, photographs from 1992. He can't tell me that during the cross-examination. This is something that must be cleared up by the other side, the source of the photographs and the approximate date of the destruction of those religious buildings, because if we trip up at the start of his testimony with no dates, no photographs, in 1992 he didn't take the pictures, what can we do with all that, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as we're seeing a series of pictures relating to buildings that are lightly damaged, heavily damaged, almost destroyed, could you tell us each time in what year these pictures were taken? That is very important. And according to what you were able to assess and what you were unable to assess, according to you, during which period was the church lightly damaged, heavily damaged, almost destroyed. We need two dates. We need the date of the photograph and the date of the assessment, if you know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best would be to return to the previous photograph, because the objection related to the previous photograph, two questions. The picture on the right-hand side, when was this taken, and when did the destruction occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in my report, in the database for which you have a printout, for every site, source information and date is given for every photograph, as well as supplementary information of various kinds. In order to simplify things, these were merely cited as descriptive examples of what I mean by damage categories. They were not intended as exhaustive documentation on any given site. If you wish, I can provide dates of destruction and sources of photographs, but it will slow things down inevitably, because I will have to look in the database. For the 178 entries, I have several hundred photographs, and I don't have necessarily have in mind the date for each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, maybe it would be easier, every time we see a picture on the screen, maybe you could tell us that the information is in the report on such-and-such a page, and then we will be able to read the additional information provided in support of what the witness is saying. For instance, the photograph we see in front of us, where we have documents 04692979 and following which relate to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will endeavour to do that, and perhaps during the next break my colleague will annotate the slide show for me so that we can provide that information to the Chamber with respect to each picture. But, again, as Mr. Riedlmayer has said, all of this information is contained in the database. But we will endeavour to put that information, the page number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could, then, please go to the next example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an example of a building that is almost destroyed. The -- you can see once again that it has suffered multiple damage. It's a Catholic Church in Stup, which is a suburb of Sarajevo, in the Ilidza Municipality. The photos, I believe, were taken during the war, and they come from published sources, and they show basically the church is burned out, there is extensive damage to the steeple, and there's damage also to the apse wall. I saw the church for the first time in the summer after the end of the war. It was still an empty shell. It has since been reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, if he hasn't seen the document in the binder, we have the photograph. This was taken by Kim Alagic [phoen] in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you could perhaps then go, Mr. Riedlmayer, to the next example.

This is a much more severe example. It's a mosque in the village of Ahatovici, in the Sarajevo suburb of Novi Grad, and Novi Grad Rajlovac; and you can see the massive stump of the minaret, identified as such, and it is basically the only identifiable element left standing. If you get the next slide, you can see what's left of the rest of the mosque, which is not very much. You can see, in the left-hand side of the rubble, a decorative column which came from the interior of the mosque. You can also see that the surrounding houses are repaired, but left standing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you explain to us, Mr. Riedlmayer, in light of the extensive damage that we've seen in these last two photographs, how it is that you've characterized these as "almost destroyed"?

"Almost destroyed" means there is still some identifiable element of the building left above ground. The totally destroyed character means just that, it means that it is either a shapeless mass of rubble or that the rubble has been cleared and the site has been levelled, in which case the only way you can identify that what was there before was a mosque, or a church, or other kind of monument, is through supplementary documentation, pre-war photos, extracts from cadastral registers, or other information, and I'll show some examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could then please go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I would like to keep the previous photograph on the screen, please. For your information, Mr. Seselj, in the document we have concerning this particular mosque, the expert refers to the testimony of Mr. Ramiz Mujikic in the Krajisnik case, page 7947 of the transcript, where the witness mentions this mosque. With this, you might be able to find your way around the slide show. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, can you start, Mr. Riedlmayer, by telling us about the characteristics of this categorisation: "Completely destroyed"?

"Completely destroyed" is a building for which no identifiable elements are left standing. In this case, the rubble is identifiable if you know what the minaret looks like, but it's certainly not left standing. It means that the building has been essentially razed and has no potentially salvageable elements left. This is a mosque in Donja Mi soca. It is a village in Ilijas, one of the Sarajevo suburbs, and you can see there isn't really much left, other than rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we perhaps go to the next example, please?

Okay. This is an example of a mosque of which really nothing is left. It is the mosque in the centre of the town of Bosansk Samac, the Aziziya Mosque built in the 19th century, and you can see the pre-war photo at left. In the photo at right, the mosque stood where the large garbage container is now standing. The tree to the left of the garbage container, I believe, is the same as the tree in the photo before. It is quite common for mosques in Bosnia to have a Linden tree or, as they call it in Bosnia, "lipa," planted next to a mosque. It's traditional to do that. Not only has the mosque been destroyed and the rubble removed, but according to the Imam of the mosque, whom I interviewed and whose statement is reproduced in the report, the Serb-controlled municipality subsequently allowed buildings, like the purple one you see on the right, to be -- to encroach on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could perhaps go to the next example.

Okay. This is an example of a building that I had to document from cadastral registers. It is in the town of Nevesinje, which is in Herzegovina, in the south of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is the Roman Catholic Perish Church. It was also a registered monument, and it was quite a lovely building. And you see a before picture published from a photograph taken in the 1980s, and at the right you see the church itself. It's the one building with the cross on it. There's a set of stairs coming down, and a crooked line is a stone wall which you will see on the next picture. The next picture was taken from roughly where the label on the street is, so slightly to the left of the church. You can see the stone wall and the empty site of the church. So the church, according to my informant, who is again quoted in the report, the parish priest himself who used to be the priest of this church, was destroyed in 1992 with explosives and the rubble taken out of town. And since then, a road has been constructed partway through the site. You can see it behind the wall there, leading to the town hospital behind the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when was this photograph taken?
This is a photograph I took in July of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps we have time before the break for one more example. If we could go to the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, may we have the previous photograph put back on the screens so that we can see that same wall by the church while the church was still standing and not destroyed. I don't remember having seen the wall. Perhaps I'm wrong, but I'd like to see the picture. So where's the wall here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right in the bottom half of the picture, near the midline. There's a set of stairs coming down from the church to the street, and then a dotted line coming around. I believe that is it. The straight lines are property lines.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, don't show me excerpts from the land registry, but on the photograph, where is the wall on the photograph? Don't refer to the sketch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. On the photograph, you cannot see it. What you can see in front of the church is the beginnings of the stairs which head down from it, but the wall would be below the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in the cadastral plan, there are no walls around the church. The plot is marked. Those lines mark the boundaries of the plot. The wall would have been marked in a different way. There probably were some stairs in front of the church, but the wall is not here either. I'm not challenging that this church might have been destroyed, but you can't now present something that is not evidence taken at the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with all due respect, these are all issues that could be raised during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, these are typically questions that you should ask during the cross-examination. We noted that there is a wall, that on the picture here we hardly see this wall. Fine. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Please go to the final example and then we'll take the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us about this slide, Mr. Riedlmayer?

This is a case where you can still see the foundations, but the building is gone. The grainy black-and-white photo at left is a published photo taken before the war of the new mosque, Dzedid Dzamija in the town of Janja near Bijeljina. It was one of two mosques in Janja, which were both destroyed in 1993. And at right of the photo, I took a photograph of the foundations. You can get some scale of it from the people standing at right. In many cases, the foundation was no longer there, but in this case you can tell that these were the dimensions of the building before it was destroyed. I again have statements from the local Islamic community, who were present in town when the mosque was destroyed, according to their account, by an explosion and the rubble removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I actually misspoke, Your Honours. If I could, I have one more example, and then that would actually be the best place to take the first break. So if we could go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. One last example, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let us go back to this photograph. You can see the contour of the hill behind this mosque, that's what it looks like to me, and here the hills seem to have been razed to the ground, not only the mosque. We can see some other buildings here, and you can see the contours of the hill on the other photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it is true that the photograph you took here on the right-hand side is such that you can't compare anything with the photo on the left-hand side. That's obvious. The new buildings were not there at the time. The environment has changed. Now, maybe on this day, it was sunny and you could really see the hills in the background, but the photograph on the right does not seem to correspond to the photograph on the left.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, what you describe as a hill is actually an artefact. It comes from a book with rather thin pages. Up near the minaret, you can see the lines of writing showing through from the previous page, and what you take to be a hill is actually an illustration on the previous page showing through. Janja is a town in the Semberija plain. It has no hills, it is a very flat area. And unfortunately, I had to work with whatever documentation I could find. This was the only pre-war published photo I could find of this mosque. If I'd been able to find better documentation, I would have included it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your document, you say that Mr. Salko Basevic, president of the Islamic Community, who told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this supposedly has been destroyed in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could just very quickly look at the next and final example from the slide show of complete "Completely destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Riedlmayer, what is depicted in this photograph?

I just wanted to include an example where all you could really find, there was no more foundation present, and all you could really find was traces of the foundation which you could look at through differences in the colour of the ground, in the type of vegetation, and you could actually outline the building that way, because the building has been completely destroyed and the rubble removed. This was the mosque in Gornji Sepak, a village north of Zvornik, and as you can see, there wasn't much visible left of it. I would have had trouble finding it, had I not had the guidance of the local imam.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. This would be an appropriate time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, before turning to the next part of the slides, can you please, if it's possible, give us some numerical conclusions regarding your report and your findings, in terms of overall destruction?

Yes. So you will recall the five categories of damage. In the survey, we -- the survey included a total of 101 mosques, which was the largest category of monuments, out of which only ten were lightly damaged. The rest were either severely damaged or destroyed. In -- with regard to Catholic churches, the percentages were similar, but the numbers were somewhat smaller, given that the Catholics are a smaller minority, and in some of the municipalities, such as Zvornik, they are not represented. Out of 27 Catholic churches, 6 Catholic monasteries, one seminary and sundry other Catholic structures, 82 per cent had been severely damaged or destroyed. Is that enough?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, if we could then please then go to the next slide, and I'd like to ask you, sir, if you were able to gather any kind of information from your site visits and documentation concerning damage.

Yes. So in addition to the documentary evidence which I've already cited, such as photographs, or informant statements, or cadastral registers and so forth, I, of course also relied on the evidence of my eyes, especially during the site visits, which in many cases was sufficient to allow me to make certain common-sense conclusions about these buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you could also now, looking at the slide that we currently see -- could you please tell us what -- read the caption so that Dr. Seselj can understand what this shows?
The text at left says: "The clues gathered from the damage."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, sir, this photograph that we see, what does this depict?

All right. This is the stump of a minaret, the base of a minaret, in the village of Ravne, south of Zvornik, in the Kamenica Valley. What you're looking at is a stump roughly two metres high. I stood next to it, and it was a little taller than me. And what is characteristic about it is the kind of damage it has suffered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'll ask you about that in just a moment. Your Honours, if you go to ERN page 0469-2781 in the annex containing the database, there's information concerning this mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know, Mr. Riedlmayer, when this photograph was taken?
I believe this is a photograph that was taken in 2002. I'd have to double-check. What was the number again?
Oh, yes. Okay. This was taken in May of 2002, by an ICTY investigator. I visited the same site in July of 2002 and saw much the same, but I liked this photo because of what it shows.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And before we turn to this minaret --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Expert, please, you said something in passing which attracted my attention. You said that this picture had been taken by an investigator of the OTP. Is this what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you there also when the picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not there when this picture was taken. I was there two months later, however, and saw the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. If one day you do another expert report for I don't know whom, normally the expert should take the picture, in order to make sure that no one can think that the person taking the picture is taking it under a certain angle for some reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my report, Your Honour, you will see an extensive appendix on the various sources of information. The photos I took were only a subset of that information. I acquired photos and other information from other sources judged to be reliable. All sources are indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I'm asking you to order Mr. Mundis that every time he tells you, the Trial Chamber, at what page the information about the destroyed building is concerned is to be found, to tell me the reference in Serbian, because I can't leaf through this binder every time. And the Prosecutor is not examining the witness following the same order, so I can't find it. It is not in the order that it is listed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, when you're giving a page, give us a number. And since the text is in English, please read it in English so that the interpreters can translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will do the best I can, Mr. President. Obviously, we're trying to move as expeditiously as possible, but I will endeavour to provide that. Of course, these slides were given to Mr. Seselj yesterday, so that he did have time to compare the slides to the report, but I will do what I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, before we turn --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, the Prosecutor cannot say that I had enough time to study this, if this was disclosed to me yesterday. I planned to study this in the two and a half hours that I waited here for the transportation. Had I been on time, I would perhaps have been able to study it, but I don't want to study anything that is in the English language. It is at the sink -- in the sink in my cell. That's where I left it. I have to get the reference where the description is in the attachment to the report in the Serbian language, because all the buildings are listed here related to the relevant locations, but the Prosecutor is not examining the witness in the same order in which they are put here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mr. Mundis said he will endeavour to meet your request. He will give you, in his own language, elements of information, and it will be translated into your language by the interpreters. As for yesterday, it is true that you did have to wait extensively before going back to your cell, but that was because of the fire in the jail. You were not the only one in this situation. Furthermore, at my request, the Registry have given me a table giving us, since the beginning of the case, when you arrived and when you left the Tribunal. I have it here in detail, and I haven't had time yet to check exactly what happened, to see whether at any point in time you were asked to wait a bit too long. I haven't had time to do this yet, but I will do this as soon as I can. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Before returning to this -- the remains of this minaret, Mr. Riedlmayer, can you just tell us a little bit about what a minaret is and what it symbolizes? What's the symbolic value of a minaret?

A minaret is a tall, slim steeple. It is located next to a mosque. It is used to signal the times of prayer. It is usually a hollow structure with a circular stairwell inside.
