The person who announces the call of the prayer, the mujezin, climbs up the stairs and goes out on a balcony and recites the call to prayer. Symbolically in a community, a minaret is often the tallest object in the village or in the neighbourhood, and it symbolizes several things, even to non-observant Muslims, it signals the presence of a Muslim community. To religious Muslims, it symbolizes many things, amongst which it points towards heaven and symbolizes the oneness of God. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, a little bit about how minarets are typically constructed in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

One has to distinguish between the minarets of traditional buildings, which are built out of stone or brick, and more modern minarets, which tend to be built with reinforced concrete. This is a fairly modern mosque and was built with the iron reinforcing rods of reinforced concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know that, sir?

If you look carefully at the photo, you will see the rods are still there. They are bent and dangling down. If you look near the top, you can see that each of the strips of masonry is hanging down from one or more bent iron rods. What you see facing towards you is what used to be the inside facing of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could pull up -- we have another still of this photograph which bears ERN number -- or 65 ter number 00463B, 00463B. It's the same photograph. We're unable to have the witness mark, Your Honours, electronically on the Powerpoint slides. This is the same slide, and I'm going to ask the witness if he can make some markings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I have to repeat an objection that I've already made. After a while, I have been able to find the information about this mosque that was destroyed, and it says here that the mosque was destroyed in February 1993. The conflict in Zvornik started on the 6th -- or, rather, the 8th of April and lasted until the 26th of April, 1992. This is a public trial, and in the interests of the public it is very important to stress this information, to present the information. If the expert has this information, and obviously he does in this case, it has to be noted in accordance with the data available to the expert. The mosque was destroyed in February of 1993, that should be enough, but you have to see my point of view. I cannot, in my cross-examination, deal with each and every building that was destroyed individually. I don't have the technical capabilities as the Prosecution has. The examination-in-chief has to put the basic information in, and the most important information is when the building was destroyed. Some of the buildings were destroyed after the Dayton Peace Agreement was signed, and that's what the expert says, himself, in his report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let me answer what you said. During a trial, we have the Prosecution that has its own witnesses, and then you have your own Defence witnesses. During the examination-in-chief of a Prosecution witness, unless major objection, the accused and his counsel will say nothing and wait for the cross-examination. During the cross-examination, you can challenge the Prosecutor's case on this specific point that you just raised. You are right, the building, as it is and as mentioned, was destroyed by explosives and razed to the ground in February 1993, after April 1992, which is when the fighting occurred in Zvornik and around Zvornik. So here there may be a problem. But during cross-examination, without going into details, you can say, in passing, that regarding this building, there is a problem, since the expert said that the building was destroyed in February 1993. This is all you should do. But if you keep raising objections over and over again during the examination-in-chief, when the Prosecutor is putting forward his case, just objecting that you cannot defend yourself alone because you have no help and so forth and so on, this is not a valid objection, and Mr. Mundis is right to reply in the way he replies. It is true you're in a difficult situation. You're self-representing yourself and assuring your own defence, and you're probably flooded with thousands and millions of documents. I understand that you have to get ready, you have to prepare. It is true you have other things going on. I fully understand that. Everything is very complicated. We're fully aware of the fact, and maybe this is why other Trial Chambers had decided to appoint a counsel for you. But you're self-representing yourself. The Trial Chamber has recognised this right, and we understand that this self-representation entails difficulties. Fine. Mr. Mundis, please, could you please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, if you could take the electronic pen that's attached to the screen. And, sir, you were telling us a few moments ago about the structure of this minaret as it was constructed, and I'm asking you now if you're able or in a position to make any markings on this photograph that would help explain that.

I will do my best. I will do what I can. Imagine the minaret having walls like this going up [marks], and the structure is held up by iron rods which before the destruction stuck up like that [marks]. They enclose a hollow space in which there is a circular stairwell. The entrance was on the other side, and there were steps going up. At some point, a blast occurred within that enclosure of the iron rods, bending them outwards and breaking them, and then the weight of the attached masonry pulled the remaining rods downwards, almost like a wilted flower, in a circular pattern [marks]. I don't pretend to be a munitions expert, but I think this is a common-sense conclusion, that there would have been an explosion placed at some distance up the steps, because there is almost two metres of the minaret still left standing. So I concluded from this that this minaret was destroyed by explosives being placed within it. And I don't know if it's my place to note it, but in fact, while the fighting in the town in Zvornik did occur in April of 1992, this particular mosque, as several other mosques in my survey, were in the Kamenica Valley south of Zvornik, which saw continued fighting into 1993. So it's not correct that the fighting in this area had stopped by 1993. I know this from my reading of standard sources on the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, this photo that you've depicted, where, as you've described it, a wilted flower or a wilting flower, those concrete reinforcing bars, are they visible in this photograph?
Yes. You can see them quite clearly between these two lines here, for example [marks]. You can see several bent bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Can you please mark that area that you've just encircled or --
[Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please now to the side draw the number 1 next to that?
[Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the concrete or the original structure, the lines that you've drawn, can you please mark a "2" next to those?
[Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And with respect to what you've described as the bars in a wilted flower, can you please indicate that with the number 3?
[Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. We would ask that this be admitted into evidence, this marked photograph, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P444.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could then please go back to the slide show. If we could go back to Sanction, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, again, for the benefit of the Chamber, this photograph or this structure is described on page 0469-2719, and the information therein indicates this photograph was taken in July 1990. And the Serbian version, we're just pulling up -- While we're doing that perhaps, Mr. Riedlmayer, can you tell us about this building and the conclusions you reached?

Yes. This is the old mosque or the Ljubovic Mosque in the village of Odzak, south of Nevesinje. It's an 18th century mosque. The pre-war photo comes from a dated publication, a magazine, published in 1990. It is a frontal view of the mosque. It is a little deceptive, because what you see up front is the low roof of a portico, a porch, that comes down almost to a man's height, and then in front a white line is a wall in front of it. Many of the older mosques in Bosnia have an overflow area in front of the door which is used on major holidays or on Fridays, when there is an overflow congregation, and they extend the roof in order to provide shelter from the weather. So that's the pre-war photo. Next to it is a document that I obtained from the former chief imam of the Islamic community in Nevesinje. It is a copy of a memorandum that he sent to the commander of the JNA at the time that this particular mosque was destroyed in 1991, and the 25th of September. This is a photo that I took of the same mosque in the summer of 2002. You can see the same supports of the sloping roof, and you can see that the minaret and the entire mosque behind the front wall is completely gone. You see also a few large blocks of stone up front. I walked around the perimeter of the site and found huge stones from the mosque, the size of this witness stand, thrown at a distance of 50 or more metres away from it. So it was a very massive explosion. And from the evidence of the remains, it appears that the explosion was within the mosque, rather than in front of it. According to the memorandum from the imam, the mosque was destroyed by JNA reservists who were on their way to the fighting in Croatia in 1991. The war in Bosnia had not officially gotten underway yet, and this was one of the first monuments that was attacked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was 25 September 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The question of relevance must be raised here. What does this have to do with the indictment against me, what does this have to do with the role of the Serbian Radical Party? The witness himself has told you that this was before the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He said that the JNA reservists were passing through in the night between the 23rd and the 24th of September, 1991. That was during the war for Serbian Krajina, and there was no fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it certainly goes to the issue of a pattern of conduct or -- and it goes to the contextual elements in which the indictment was raised. Perhaps this type of objection would be better placed when we get to the point where I will be tendering the entire report into evidence, and I can address Your Honours then as to any of the specific examples contained in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My case manager, Your Honours, is endeavouring, to the best of her ability sitting here, to try to locate the corresponding Serbian language pages of the annex, and I will tell you, with all transparency, that in realtime it's not going to be possible for us to do that. If it's important for the accused to have the Serbian language page numbers of the annex with respect to the dates of the photographs, then I'm going to ask for a recess in order to allow us to go through the multiple hundred-page -- hundreds of pages of annexes and pull up the Serbian language page numbers. So if the Chamber directs us to provide that information in realtime as we go along, I am going to be forced to ask for a recess in order to do that. I've got -- I'm approximately halfway done with the slides, so I don't want to continue having objections about the information that Dr. Seselj says he needs, but I cannot sort through this myself, standing here in court. So I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands, but those would seem to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Continue, continue as you started. We will assess this on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could then go to the next slide. This is contained in the English version of the annex at page 0469-2784, and according to the information contained therein, this photograph or these photographs were taken in July 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, Mr. Riedlmayer, what's depicted in these two photographs?

Yes. This is another mosque in the Kamenica Valley, south of Zvornik, Zvornik Municipality. It is in a village called Redzici, and it is quite plain, what you're looking at. It is a somewhat older mosque made out of stone, and the mosque is burned out. Even from the photos, you can see that it is missing its roof and the interior is empty. I actually went inside, and I saw charred room timbers. The distinguishing feature here is that the stone minaret is not only decapitated, and you can see the signs of a blast simply not only from missing stonework but from the large fissure in the stone work, but the cap of the minaret, the balcony, landed inside the stump. And, you know, again, you have to conclude that this happened through some fairly major blast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, I'd be grateful if you would just give us two pieces of information in relation to each of these pictures; namely, when was the church or the mosque destroyed, and when was the photo taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. The photo was taken during my fieldwork in July of 2002. And according to the statement from the informant who accompanied me to this, the former head imam of the main mosque in Zvornik, the mosque was damaged by shelling in June of 1992 and was destroyed in October 1992, when this particular village fell to the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please then go to the next slide, and this corresponds to page -- the ERN number is 0469-2977. And again, Mr. Riedlmayer, if you can explain to us what is depicted here, taking into consideration the information that Judge Harhoff has also requested, please.

The photograph at the left is a pre-war photo. It was taken in 1980, and it comes from the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, an organisation based in Geneva, which awarded the restoration of the old town of Mostar with the Aga Khan award in 1980. What it shows is the mosque of Koski Mehmed Pasha. It is the largest and most visible mosque in the old town centre of Mostar. The picture was taken from very near the famous Old Bridge in Mostar, and it is from almost but not quite the same angle of view as the second photo. The second photo was taken in August of 1992 by a professional photographer named Paul Harris, who then published it in a volume of his photographs entitled: "Cry Bosnia." The sources are indicated in the bibliography entry to the database entry. The difference between the points of view is merely that in the pre-war photo, the photographer was standing higher up at the edge of the ravine, whereas in the post-war photo he was a little bit lower down, and so you see a little more of the mountain behind. But otherwise, it's a very similar angle. And since it was August of 1992, we know the damage had to come from the first siege of Mostar. What you see is that the mosque has been impacted several times by projectiles. The minaret has been cut off near the base. There are several holes through the wall of the mosque and through the dome, and at least one of the nearby buildings has also been hit. Next slide. Okay. These are two close-up views from a volume of documentation on damage to the architecture at Mostar, published in 1992 by the Federation of Architects of Mostar. The photograph at the left is the base of the minaret. You can see where it has been sheared off, and next to it you can also see the entrance, portico, and part of it has been caved in either by the projectile or the falling masonry. You would enter the mosque through that portico, and at right is the image within the mosque. You can see the hole in the dome and one of the holes in the walls of the mosque, and you can see the considerable damage it has already suffered through rain and other elements coming in. The dark areas spreading near the holes indicate the damp damage. So this is a monument that I called "heavily damaged" in the categorisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, Mr. Riedlmayer, this mosque that's depicted on this slide is the same mosque that we saw in the previous slides from across the river?
Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could then go to the next slide. This --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I really cannot follow this. It's quite impossible. I have to be given the page in Serbian, because I just spend all my time leafing through and I still can't find it, and I haven't managed to find this last mosque. Now, if you consider that I don't need to follow this, I'll take my headset off and let matters take their course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, the accused has the binder, like we do. The photograph we have before us has a page number in the binder, so please give us this number. Just specify that the photograph is in the binder, give us a page number, and, Mr. Seselj, in the binder you turn to the page number in question. What is the page number?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, are you referring to the Registry page number on the top of these pages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the number which is on the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, the slide, Your Honours, we're now showing is page 39 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand. In the binder, there are numbers, the pages are numbered, so give him the page number in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's page number 39 in the e-court version, and the page number -- the hard page number is page 633/12459 ter. The top right-hand corner. The English version of this slide on the left bears ERN number 0469-2584, and the photo on the right bears ERN number 0469-2583.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I'm concerned, page 633 was sufficient information. I found it straight away. That's all I need the Prosecutor to tell me, just the page in the Serbian version. And as soon as he said, "Page 633," I found it straight away, and that's the simplest way to do it, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you had said, "Page 583," personally I would --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "533" in my book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the pages are not numbered the same way in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, they're not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Well, yes, of course. So please give us the number in B/C/S, please, the B/C/S page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We will again endeavour to do that, to the extent we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, looking at the two photos on the screen in front of you, can you tell us, sir, what is depicted in these photographs, again keeping in mind the information Judge Harhoff requested?

Okay. The two photos both come from the president of the Islamic Community of Janja, Mr. Salko Basevic, whom I interviewed in July of 2002. The left-hand photo was taken before the war. It shows the Atik Dzamija or old mosque in the center of Janja. You will note two characteristic features. One is the gate house at the left and the other one is the rhombus-shaped window on the mosque. The photograph on the right was taken in April of 1993, and it shows the mosque the morning after it was blown up, and it shows, first of all, the great amount of rubble in front. In the back, you can see part of the wall, but the minaret is gone. But you can still see the rhombus-shaped windows. You can also see the force of the blast sheared off the top of the tall tree in front of the mosque. And at the far right of the picture, you can see a yellow bulldozer in the act of clearing the rubble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: On the slide that's now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. I'd like us to remain on this slide. Don't let them move on, because the Prosecutor wants to keep something back, and nothing should be kept back from the public. Look at the end of the text. The witness says here that he heard that the destruction of this mosque was the act of extremist part of the police force called "The Panthers," whom members we saw on the streets, and their commander was Major Mauser, and he asked by the 15th of April, all Muslims leave Bijeljina. So we're talking about 1993 here, one year after the battle for Bijeljina. And I would like to remind you, Mr. President, when you were the Pre-Trial Judge, and previously when other Judges took your place, I asked that under 68(1) I be disclosed all the Ljubisa Mauser, Panthers documents, who was the vice-prime minister of Djindjic in his party and set up the party in Republika Srpska and for the Serbian guards of Vuk Draskovic, and I still haven't been disclosed that material, and for the public, the Prosecutor has to state that because I am being held accountable for that crime, so I have to intervene. This is not a question for cross-examination, I am not going to deal with it in cross-examination, I have a different concept for my cross-examination, but the Prosecutor must not hide or keep back important facts. The witness has just indicated the perpetrator of a crime, according to what the local said, the imam of the mosque or whoever. I can't be specific on that point. I can't find it now, but anyway, and the public is left with the impression that I destroyed that mosque, and you must believe me when I say that I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, according to the witness, this was destroyed by the Panthers of this famous Mauser. Mr. Seselj had already asked, and I remember this, to have everything relating to this group of individuals disclosed to him. Was this done, was this not done? I know nothing about this. You have attributed this destruction to him. As I said yesterday, when I commented on the indictment, I said to Mr. Seselj that he could be held responsible for crimes committed by others, insofar as these other individuals were part of the same criminal enterprise as he was. I don't know whether this group was part of the criminal enterprise or not. But Mr. Seselj is challenging this. He is saying that this was done by others that have nothing to do with him. This is my first question. The documents relating to Mauser's Panthers, were these documents disclosed to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not in a position to answer that question right now. I would certainly make the inquiries. I would ask, with all due respect, that these interventions by the accused be stopped. This has to do very little with this witness and his testimony. We are trying to move through this expert's report as expeditiously as possible. The issues raised by the accused, with respect to disclosure, is a matter that could be dealt with a little bit later, and the argumentation that he puts forward concerning the Panthers is certainly something that is not appropriately done at this stage of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Without going into the substance of this, who did what? In your expert report, you mentioned an article which was published in "Newsday" in New York. This article describes what happened. Did you look into the matter, did you try to understand who did what, or did you not deal with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I included any firsthand news reports, mainly to settle issues as to when something was destroyed. It was really not in my competence to carry out investigations about individual parties responsible. And I will note that the information I got from Mr. Basevic is all on the very first page. That's page 583. The rest of the information, one is a piece of witness testimony from a transcript in the Milosevic trial, and there are three excerpts from news reports. The Gottman [phoen] article from "Newsday" is significant mainly for noting that as of February 1993, the mosque was still standing, and the ones by the reporters from the "London Independent" and the "Washington Post" show that by the first week of May, it was no longer standing. That was my main goal in including those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, the Prosecutor seems to want to establish for the time being that this was destroyed. For the time being, the witness will not talk about who has destroyed it. You could have raised your objections during your cross-examination. This is another issue. This witness is coming here today to say that the mosques have been destroyed, full stop. He doesn't know who has destroyed these mosques.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... here that no article is quoted. It is a television programme, in fact, by journalist -- his name is G.B. Rado from Independent Television news, and he is reporting from the town at the point in time when the mosque is being destroyed. And you can see that mayor of Bijeljina, Jovan Vojnovic, a Serb, at the end explains to him that he learned about the plans to destroy the mosque in advance and that he was opposed to them. And then he said, with the sounds of a bulldozer in the background, he speaks of the impossibility of him doing anything. And this is a component part of the expert report. The expert report must necessarily contain information about each of the religious buildings, who destroyed it and when, and we don't have that information for each of these buildings. And secondly bear in mind that Zoran Djindjic and Ljubisa Savic Mauser are not mentioned in any indictment as participants in the joint criminal enterprise. Had it said that Slobodan Milosevic had destroyed this mosque, since I am part of the joint criminal enterprise, accused of such with him, then I would be responsible with him and instead of him now. But as it says that Mauser did that, then Djindjic cannot respond, nor can Mauser. They were never in a joint criminal enterprise, and I can't be held responsible for the two of them. Although they don't exist, but find someone, a third person, who will be held accountable for Djindjic's and Mauser's crimes. So this objection is rather complex. It has to do with relevance. When something is irrelevant, then I have the right to intervene at any point. Secondly, it has to do with the comprehensiveness of this expert report. This expert isn't an author and just travelogue and describes what he just saw, but he enters into an analysis of what was destroyed and who destroyed it. Sometimes he's successful and sometimes he's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you take the floor, it's an avalanche of issues you raise now, one cannot prevent you from defending yourself, so I have to state things as they stand. This expert report was disclosed to your experts, who are present in the courtroom today. What you have just said you could have mentioned in the submissions you filed after having received this expert report, so it is needless to repeat what has been said all right. We know the public at large, of course, doesn't know that this has been mentioned in your submissions, but then wait for the cross-examination. You mentioned this third point. You reproach the expert who is sitting in front of us for not having looked into the issue of who did what. His assignment at the time was not to say who had done what. He was there to see what had happened. He was not there to authenticate the perpetrators. If it's Mr. Mauser who is responsible, this was not -- this is not part of the examination-in-chief of this witness. That is another issue. I understand that you mention your responsibility in the matter, which is perfectly understandable, but choose the right witness. This witness cannot say who did what. He went there, he took photographs, he spoke to people, but he did not conduct any investigations of a police or judicial nature, so he can't say who did what. He just, as you can see on reading his report, compiled a series of articles, wrote down what one or another person told him, and that's all he did. We will have to admit or not admit his expert report. As far as we are concerned, the only important issue is this: On the basis of the information provided in the report and the questions put by the Prosecutor, the answers provided by the witness, the questions put by you and the answers provided by the witness again, will this warrant the admission of his report and the annexes. It is not a matter of trying to understand who did what. This issue will be addressed with other witnesses at another point in time. Mr. Mundis, can you confirm that this witness is here today to only talk about the fact that mosques and churches were destroyed; he's not here today to say X, Y, Z has done this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The witness explained the taskings he was given. The Trial Chamber will be asked, at the end of all the evidence in this case, to reach the ultimate decisions that must be made, based on all the evidence they've heard. That would include this expert's report. That would include this expert's testimony, in our respectful views. But we again -- as the Presiding Judge just indicated, we need to be moving forward and focusing on all of the evidence. And if this is not the right witness to be putting certain things to, then we should not allow that to happen. What we're trying to do is move as expeditiously as possible. I would ask that the interventions and objections of the accused be subtracted from his cross-examination time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, I must be very watchful here and watch what Mr. Seselj is doing, but I need to watch over you, too. I have put to you a very clear question, and you did not answer my question. This is my question: This is an expert witness. Is he here today to come and testify about the destructions that occurred in churches and mosques, and is not here to talk about the perpetrators of these destructions? And I await your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness, in his report, has cited to information concerning the destruction of these buildings and, in some instances, the perpetrators. The Trial Chamber can give that information whatever weight it deems necessary, after hearing all of the evidence. It may be that at the end of the trial, when all the evidence is in, some of the cited material that Mr. Riedlmayer cites to concerning the perpetrators the Chamber will give no weight to. I'm not in a position to say what weight, if any, should be given to the material cited to in his database or the annex, because we haven't heard all the evidence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you remind the Trial Chamber what the exact field of expertise of this witness was? In other words, a letter which was sent to him, asking him to provide this report, what exactly did you ask of him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The witness has explained that, Your Honour. He was asked to look at the destruction of cultural property in the relevant municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, relating to the indictment in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He wasn't asked to authenticate the perpetrators of these destructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, he was not. During the course of his fieldwork, as he's testified, a number of -- on a number of occasions information was provided to him, and he has included that in the database. Whether it was from an open source, whether it was from a journalist, whether it was from a priest, whether it was from an imam, that information at the end of the trial the Chamber may give some weight to, having heard all the evidence in the case. But, of course, it's certainly hearsay with respect to what people told him outside of the courtroom or what he read in a contemporaneous media report or a book. But once you've heard all of the evidence, the Chamber may then decide, "We'll give certain weight to the database information or the report, but we'll give weight to other things concerning the evidence." The primary thrust of the report concerns the destruction of cultural property in the relevant locations during the relevant time periods.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President and Judges, for each of the destroyed or damaged buildings, the witness states who destroyed it to the best of his knowledge. There are always second-hand, third-hand, or fourth-hand stories but he says something everywhere in all instances; and the most general formulation is Serb forces, that's the term that is used, then extremists from amongst the Serb ranks, I assume he means the buildings that were destroyed outside combat. Then he mentions Mauser's Men or the Panther's, and in some places, he uses the term "Arkan's men." He never says "Volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party" or "Seselj's men." And you notice very well that an investigation must be launched into who actually did destroy these buildings. Now, the question is: Who is to conduct that investigation? Is it up to the Prosecutor or is it only up to me? I am fully convinced that it is only the Prosecutor who can conduct an investigation, because I am not here to prove my innocence. I am protected by the presumption of innocence, so it is up to the Prosecutor to prove and show evidence that I destroyed these. He did offer up certain evidence through this witness -- through this expert report, but they're not sufficient, because we can see there was never a real investigation. But they are an indicator. I know you can't take this at face value, any of the observations by the expert as to who did the destruction, but they could be indicators as to who could be suspects or suspected of having destroyed these buildings, at the very least. And now you expect in the Defence cross-examination for me to say that I did not destroy mosques and churches. I'm not going to do that, and in fact I'm reaching a decision not to present my Defence case at all. I'll leave it up to the Prosecutor, what the Prosecutor says I did. We'll leave it at that. I don't want to prove that I'm innocent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Expert, please, could you please tell the Trial Chamber what was the purpose of your report? You wrote this report, so you must know exactly what was the purpose of your report. What was your assignment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of my report was to provide information on the destruction of cultural property in the designated municipalities, with a focus on the cultural property of the Muslim and Roman Catholic communities. This information would include information on the buildings, when they were destroyed, in what state they were when I saw them, and any other information that seemed relevant to the destruction that I was able to gather from various sources during the course of my investigation. Everything that I put into the database and into the report is very carefully sourced, and I believe it is up to this Court to evaluate that evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll stop you here. It's like hearing a representative of the OTP telling me, "It's up to you to assess." Line 2, page 70, you say: " ... and any other information that may be relevant regarding the destruction." Does this mean -- does this sentence mean that this is the reason why you mentioned identities or groups of people who, by hearsay, you were told that they were the perpetrators of these destructions? Please don't look at the OTP. Look at me, please. I'm asking the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The assignment, as I saw it, was, first of all, to make sure that any ruined building I saw had, in fact, been destroyed during the war and hadn't been either demolished after the war or before the war. I understood it to be important to establish when something was destroyed. That was the general focus of it. I will note, for example, that in the entry related to the mosque on that picture, I never referred to perpetrators in any specific term. If, however, in the course of my investigations I was told such information, I noted it down, and I thought it would be up to the OTP if it wanted to approach the witnesses or take formal depositions. That is not my role. I understood that, but I also felt that any information that I received that seemed to be substantive, I ought to include for whatever value it may carry. The obligation I felt was simply to establish whatever facts could be established or whatever information could serve towards establishing those facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for the information of the Judges and of the public, what exactly are you an expert at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm an expert -- first of all, my primary formation, I'm a historian, so a historian's impetus is to find out what happened. And in order to find out what happened, you gather various evidence. Also, for the past 24 years, I have been involved in the documentation of cultural heritage, specifically art and architecture, and I saw, as my primary task, finding out what happened to these buildings. What I was documenting primarily was, (a), the condition of the building before and after, and, (b), trying to find out some information about when it happened to that building. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was looking at what you've done up until now. On page 2623, the Catholic Church at Bosansk Samac, this is what you're adding as a caption, your comment was the following: "This church was destroyed by the Serbian forces when they attacked the village in May 1992. At least ten Catholics were killed." Is that what you were asked, to also provide information on the casualties and to say exactly what units were involved, or did you believe that because you had heard this, somebody told you it was worth noting it down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was told this by the parish priest of that church, I thought it was important information to note down, not to leave it out. But, you know, again, if he hadn't told me that, I wouldn't have been going around making inquiries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As you just saw, the Trial Chamber deliberated on this, given the objections raised and the issues raised. The Chamber will now render an oral decision. The Prosecutor, as of 11.40, can only asking the following questions to the witness: Questions dealing with the location where the destruction occurred; questions dealing with the nature of the destruction; questions dealing with the identification of the destroyed property. The Prosecutor is allowed to ask the witness whether he has information pertaining to the date at which the destruction occurred. However, regarding this fourth item, the Trial Chamber reserves itself the right to give or not give probative value to the witness's answer, according to the elements that it will have. Thus, the Prosecution is no longer required to ask specific different questions to the witness, and the witness is not supposed to answer any questions, dealing with who did what. Furthermore, Mr. Seselj's Defence will also not be allowed to involve the possible involvement of X, Z or Y to the events. The Trial Chamber is only interested in knowing where the destruction occurred, what property was destroyed, and at what date the property was destroyed. These are the different items. And if the expert actually took a picture, he must give us the dates at which the pictures were taken. If there's two pictures, the date of the first picture, the date of the second picture. We do not want to know any more than that. Now, after this oral decision, Mr. Mundis, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we can return, then, Mr. Riedlmayer, to the slide in front of you to resume. I believe before the interventions, you were telling us that there was a before-and-after shot of the Mosque of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in Janja.
Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if we can go to the next slide, can you tell us what this photo is and what it depicts?

This is a photo taken in 1992 when I visited Janja. It shows a new mosque under construction. This is in 2002, and it shows some of the surrounding houses which are part of the community of Janja. And as you can see from the neighbouring houses, the roofs are old, so they're presumably houses that date from before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could we please go to the next slide. The information concerning these photographs may be found in page 406 of the Serbian language version of the report. The English version bears ERN number 0469-2877. Can you tell us, Mr. Riedlmayer, what's depicted in these two photographs?

These two photographs are of a mosque in the village of Svrake, which is in the Sarajevo suburbs, of Vogosca in the Semizovac area. The photo on the left comes from a documentary volume that was published right after the war, and presumably the photo was taken at the end of the war. The photo at the right was taken in 2003, and I obtained it from the Islamic Community. However, I also visited the community at one point. What they both show is -- the one on the left is the damage to the mosque, and once again we are revolving 90 degrees to the left. In the photo of the destroyed mosque at the left, you see -- what you see is the same wall as the wall bathed in sunshine of the reconstructed mosque, so it's that wall. And what you see in the left-hand side of the black-and-white's picture is the remains of the minaret, the stump of the minaret. You can also see, if you look carefully, that, first of all, the roof is gone and, secondly, there are collapsed roof timbers inside. What this indicates is some sort of blast damage. The information I had as to the timing of destruction is cited in the entry for this at page 878. It includes testimony from another case before this Tribunal, the Krajisnik case, and also a Council of Europe report, and the third one is from the State Commission for Gathering Facts for War Crimes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. So three different sources. I cite them for the information of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Riedlmayer. Your Honours, this would be an appropriate spot for the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will now break for 20 minutes, and we will resume at 12.05. And let me remind you that we will sit until 1.15 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, the Registrar told me that you have used one hour and six minutes, so you have fifty-four minutes left, which means we will not finish today. Witness, unfortunately you will have to come back next Tuesday. I asked you yesterday whether it was a problem for you. Is it a problem or not? If you have commitments, we could always set another date for you to come back, but if it's possible, it would be best if you could come on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can come. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, we'll turn now to a different topic. I'm wondering, sir, if you can tell us, based upon the fieldwork that you've done and your other work concerning cultural property relating to this case, if you were in a position to observe any noticeable patterns or trends.

Yes. I made some effort to note which buildings were of the pre-modern period, so the Ottoman-Austro-Hungarian period, and also which buildings had been listed monuments, in other words, under register of protective monuments under the legislation in effect in the former Yugoslavia. And in the case of mosques, almost two-thirds of the mosques, 65 out of 101, were dated from the Ottoman or Austro-Hungarian period, and 30 of these had been designated as listed monuments. I found that these older mosques and the mosques which had been deemed of special importance, and therefore designated for listing, had been disproportionately destroyed. Overall, the degree of destruction was quite high, some 90 per cent of all mosques, but in the case of these older mosques, a much higher percentage was heavily damaged or destroyed. And, similarly, 28 out of the 30 mosques that were listed monuments were found heavily damaged, and the two that weren't, one was on the Bosnian government side of the confrontation line and was damaged by explosive projectiles, but it was not destroyed, and the other listed mosque was in Nevesinje, where two other mosques had -- and the Catholic Church had been destroyed. But this mosque was inactive. It was in the center of town, but it had lost its minaret sometime before the war and had been used as a warehouse during the communist period. It was vandalised and desecrated, but it was not destroyed, unlike the two other mosques which were completely levelled. So from this, I would conclude that these mosques had been singled out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, you're saying that these mosques were listed. Now, a layman could wonder what this means. Who listed these mosques? Was it the country, itself, listed as a cultural or religious monument, or is it a world listing, were they listed maybe to the World Heritage List or something? What exactly is -- what did you mean exactly when you said they were registered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I provide a detailed explanation, Your Honour, in footnote number 11 of my narrative report. It's attached to paragraph 23. They were listed under the legislation in effect in the former Yugoslavia. These were laws both at the federal level and at the republican level of the Federal Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what the designation meant was that these were buildings that could not, under the law, be demolished, or altered, or destroyed, and that they would be eligible for state conservation money. It's the same kind of monuments protection law you have in most European countries, and it involves a process where certain monuments are nominated and then designated. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, as a historian and someone who specialised in Islamic art and architecture in the Balkans, what's the significance of your conclusions with respect to the older particularly mosques that were destroyed or damaged?

These were the major landmarks of those particular localities, and presumably had greater cultural significance than smaller or less notable buildings that had been built more recently. I can cite as an example the mosque you see to the right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps if we go to the next slide. And before you answer that, sir, let me just again, for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom, this is page 319 of the Serbian version of the report, and the ERN number of the English is 0469-2992. Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Riedlmayer.

This is the Karadjoz Beg Dzamija, the mosque of Karadjoz Mehmed in Mostar. It was built in 1557, and it is one of the most notable pieces of Islamic sacral architecture in Bosnia, if not the Balkans. It was a listed monument. And the photograph at left, taken before the war, comes, I believe, from the Institute for the Protection of Monuments. The photograph at right comes from that same documentary volume I referred to earlier, produced by the Mostar Federation of Architects. It was taken in the summer of 1992, and it shows the damage from the first siege of Mostar. You can tell, first of all, that the minaret has been decapitated above the balcony, and you can tell there were multiple impacts on the mosque, smashing the portico. It's worth noting that this particular mosque did suffer further damage in the second siege of Mostar, but the principal damage, as to most monuments of Mostar, was done in the first siege, the one in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could then go, please, to the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, expert witness, you told us you were a historian. I'm sure you are well versed in the history of the Balkans. The destruction of religious monuments that we see here, could you tell us whether, in the history of the region, there were precedents to this, whether whenever there was a conflict, whether one of the manifestations in the conflict was to go and destroy the Orthodox Church, or the mosque, or the Catholic Church? Did you look into this? Did you look into what had happened earlier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, part of the supplementary information provided in the appendices to my report includes both my testimony before the International Court of Justice and several of my articles where I discuss this. The simple fact is that the degree of destruction that we saw in Bosnia-Herzegovina in the 1992-1995 war was, indeed, unprecedented. There had been destruction before, for example, in World War II and during the wars of the 19th century, but never at this scale. In ordinary times, these monuments very often would face each other across the town square, which if you give it consideration, is a statement of sorts. If these were people who really loathed each other and couldn't bide each other's sight, they wouldn't have expended the investment and put these monuments in such a way that they would have to face the other every time they emerged from worship. So during most of the times, it was not a problem. The other thing that is to consider is you will note that two things of these mosques date from the Ottoman and Austro-Hungarian period, meaning they survived for centuries before being destroyed or damaged in this current thing. Now, obviously in time of war, there are such things as tit-for-tat and acts of retribution. What strikes me about the pattern of destruction that I've seen in Bosnia, both in the set of municipalities for this report and for my other reports, has been the totality of the destruction in the territory that was controlled by Serb forces during the war. I know of only one mosque that survived with its minaret intact and largely undamaged. That was in one village in Bosnia, Voljine [phoen], near Mrkonjic Grad, where the local Serb residents stopped paramilitaries from destroying the mosque. But everywhere else, in major cities where these buildings were at the center of town and presumably in plain view of everyone, these were destroyed and often destroyed in the absence of any fighting. So that's the pattern I've seen. Yes, there was destruction of World War II and there was sporadic destruction going back to the 19th century, but, no, this kind of total erasure was certainly unprecedented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please then go to the next slide, and again the information concerning this cultural property is on page 304 in the Serbian version, and the ERN number for the corresponding English pages is 0469-3012. Can you tell us, Mr. Riedlmayer, what is depicted on the screen in front of you?

What we see here is probably the one monument in Bosnia that even people who haven't been there will recognise. It's the old Ottoman bridge over the Neretva River in Mostar, and everyone knows that the bridge was brought down in the second siege of Mostar by Croatian shelling. This, however, is a photo taken in the summer of 1992, following the first siege of Mostar by Yugoslav and Serb forces. In my database entry for this, I characterize the damage to the bridge as light. You can see there have been some impacts, also an effort to shield the bridge. Somebody has tried to put some planks across. If you bring up the next slide, please. However, there was severe damage to the two 16th century towers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Please, may we have the previous slide back on our screens and have the witness tell us on what side of the bridge this is. What's the side we're looking at? On what side of the bridge is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is proper cross-examination type of questioning. The accused, Dr. Seselj, can't object to an answer of the witness, so I would ask the Trial Chamber to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Mr. Mundis is quite right. If you wish to challenge these photographs or what these photographs look like, since the witness hasn't said anything particularly salient about it, he said that the bridge had been slightly damaged, that's it, he said that was destroyed afterwards, so please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, well, I do have something to say in this regard, with your permission. If you don't give me permission, I'm not going to do anything. I'm not going to fight for the right to say something. If you're courteous enough to allow me to say something, I will. If not, I won't. But why is this important? This is the frontline in Mostar. The Serbs were on one side, the Croats on the other. So there's nothing more important than for us to hear stated which side of the bridge this is and where the damage is done. I'm not going to deal with that during the cross-examination, but you must provide the public with precise information on this point. And, secondly, the witness is now talking about the damages done, and we see over there that there are hardly any damages, except for what was caused by rifle fire. But let's see who targeted the building we saw that was partially damaged. It was the party on the other side, on the opposite side. So let's see who was on the opposite side. You're trying people who have been charged with the destruction of this bridge, so let's not link this up with the other trial now, or let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your comment would be particularly welcome if the witness were here to say who had done what. We handed down a decision a moment ago, and we stated that the witness was to talk about the nature of the destruction and not about the perpetrators. Now, if you say which side this was on, you are already biased. This is why I don't wish to say any more about it. Technically speaking, if you look at the photograph on the Serb side, if you look on the Serb side and the Croatian side, you are quite right, but this is not our subject matter today. We want to acknowledge things visually, on the basis of the photographs shown to us by the witness. We want to assess the level of the damage. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you please comment upon the two photographs shown on the screen in front of you?

Yes. This is one of the two medieval towers that flanked the bridge on either side. What you're looking at is the left bank of the river, the east side. The river is flowing to the south. And the 1981 photograph comes from the Aga Khan Cultural, and I was able to match it up with an exact angle with a photograph taken in 1992 and published by the Mostar Federation of Architects. And if you take a look at the entry for the bridge, you will also see a detailed technical assessment of the bridge also done in 1992 by Dr. Colin Kaiser, the UNESCO representative. From what you can see just visually, you can see that the tower and its surrounding structures have been burned out and that there have been major projectile impacts upon it. If you look at Colin Kaiser's report, he expresses concerns for the structure. Nevertheless, given the reserved nature of my damage scale, I still called this "lightly damaged," and in fact they did prove to be suitable for reconstruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can we please go to the next slide, and this is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I just have a question to ask you and your colleagues. Did you hear well when it was said that this building is on the east bank of the Neretva River? That's the interpretation I got. That's all I'm interested in. Is that what you heard, too, because the witness said it's on the east bank and the Neretva River flows west of that. That's all I'm interested in, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you did say that the building was located on the east side of the Neretva; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Turning to the slide in front of us, this mosque may be -- the description of this mosque may be found in the database, page 527 of the Bosnian or Serbian version of the report, and the English ERN number 0469-2707. Mr. Riedlmayer, can you please tell us what's depicted on this screen?

Okay. This is one of the oldest mosques in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's Carev Dzamija or Mosque of the Sultan Bajezid, the second built in 1485, in the town of Nevesinje of Herzegovina. This is a photograph from a guide-book published immediately before the war and shows the mosque following a recent conservation that was carried out just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please go to the next slide. What does this photograph depict, Mr. Riedlmayer?
This is the site of the mosque when I visited it in July of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who took this photo, sir?
I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe what's depicted in the photograph, please?

If you would please go to the previous slide, I can point something out. This photo is taken downhill, looking towards the mosque. The other photo was taken uphill from the downhill end, so the mosque would have been where those junked lorries and other automobiles are. You can see the discolouration in the grass, which outlines the foundations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a piece of information. The photograph clearly shows that there are no stones left, there's nothing left of the mosque. According to you, what happened to the stones of this mosque? Were they used to build the neighbouring houses or were these stones, like this was the case for castles in France, these went to the United States ? What happened to these stones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I interviewed the imam of the mosque, Armin Effendi Omerika, who was present in Nevesinje at the start of the war, and I was told that first of all the -- he gave me a date for the destruction of the mosque, which is in the entry which I'm trying to find here. And he also told me that following the explosion, the rubble was collected and taken out of town and dumped in a garbage dump, which he then later showed us, a dump site at Ponor, two kilometres outside of Nevesinje. In fact, all that was left was the underground part of the foundations, which you could still see through the grass, but the site had been completely levelled. The surrounding houses all pre-date the war. They are older houses with roofs that have patina on them, so they weren't destroyed. And according to my information, there was no real fighting in Nevesinje. This did not happen as part of a battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Riedlmayer, on the lower right-hand side of this photograph, there's a small wall that's visible. It's less than a metre tall, I would estimate. Can you tell us what that is?

Okay. That is a graveyard that -- a family graveyard of the Basagic [phoen] family, who were the most notable Muslim family in Nevesinje, and you can see it on a pre-war photo that I also included in my database entry. At the time I visited, the gravestones were still there, but the graveyard was being used as a vegetable garden.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please go to the next slide. And, again, for the benefit of everyone in the courtroom, the Serbian version of the information concerning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Could we get back to the previous photograph, please. On looking at the previous photograph, I discover there's a white truck that has "UN" marked on it at the back, so I assume that when you went to take your pictures, you were accompanied by a member of the OTP, I assume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was accompanied by a Tribunal investigator. He's mentioned in my report, who acted as driver and security. All he did is he drove the jeep where I told him to and periodically reported back to base on a satellite phone about security. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, just very briefly. Judges, I hope that you are aware that at that time the Serbian Restoration Movement was in power in Nevesinje at that time, the SDS was not in power, the Serbian Radical Party did not exist there. This is one of the two municipalities in Republika Srpska that were governed by the Serbian Restoration Movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, that's not a proper objection or intervention at this point in time, and we would again ask that the accused be instructed to limit his objections to proper legal objections concerning questions and not to simply make comments or legal argumentation during the course of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your objection, which is of a legal nature, pertains to Article 7(1) of the Statute. This witness will not label anyone to settle the issue. You can address this matter at a different time, different moment, different place. You can perhaps address this issue in the presence of another witness. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The information concerning this mosque is found on page 633 in the Serbian version, and the ERN pages in the English version, 0469-2562 and 2563.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you tell us what's depicted in these two photographs, please?

What we are looking at is the mosque of Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent, also known as Atik dzamija or old mosque at the centre of Bijeljina. The photo at left comes from a pre-war guide book edited by Nebojsa Bato Tomasevic. It dates from 1980. The photograph at right is one I took in July of 2002. It shows the same site. All that is left, once again, of the mosque is the discolouration in the grass. The site is right in the center of town, next to the government buildings and other major monuments of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, on the picture on the right, can you tell us what is depicted in the background on the left-hand side of that photograph?
Yes. That is the Serbian Orthodox Church in the centre of Bijeljina, both the very tall bell tower and the structure to its left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on the information available to you, sir, and your fieldwork, do you know when this mosque was destroyed?
According to the information I had, and the statement is on the second page of the entry, the mosque was one of five mosques in Bijeljina that were blown up on the night of 12-13 March 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I also simply note, Your Honours, for the record, that videotape P348, which was shown on 3 April 2008, relates to this mosque. I simply point that out for the Trial Chamber's benefit. If we could please then go to the next slide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This mosque is described beginning on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a follow-up question to put to the witness. If you allow me, I'd like to see the previous slide again. Here, you see the ground in the forefront. There's nothing there, the mosque doesn't exist anymore. And in the background, you can see the Orthodox Church. There are two things that are noteworthy here. You said that this mosque had been destroyed between the 12th and the 13th of March, 1993, during the night. Some individuals, I don't know who these people are, threw an explosive, perhaps, and everything blew up. The debris then fell to the ground, and these individuals left. But how is it that later on, the mosque was not rebuilt and, (b), that everything disappeared? If everything was cleaned up, as we see it there - there's no waste paper, there's nothing lying around - the stones, the waste material, the rubble, everything was taken away, it looks like a clean slate, but who removed everything from there; not the people who threw the explosives? Who took everything away? Did you reflect on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular incident was extremely well reported in the media, not only by the television reporter whose video the Court already saw, but by other reporters who were present in town, because at the time the Republika Srpska Assembly was holding its meeting in town, deliberating on one of the peace plans, the Vance-Owen Plan, and they were all present in town when the five mosques were blown up. And according to these news reports, some of which I have included, the very day after the destruction, municipal work crews, with heavy machinery, were busy removing the stones of the mosque and levelling the site. So the removal happened in conjunction, really, with the destruction, within less than 24 hours. Following the destruction of the mosque, even after the Dayton Peace Agreement, the Islamic Community -- you asked about the rebuilding problem. The Islamic Community of Bosnia-Herzegovina sought permission to retake control of the plot of ground and to rebuild the mosque, and they brought suit before the Human Rights Chamber of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is a mixed international and local judicial body established under the Dayton Agreement. And the Human Rights Chamber brought a number of rulings on this which also concern certain facts about the destruction of the mosque, and I have appended the text of those rulings as an appendix to my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we please go to the next --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I'm surprised that you missed it. According to the information available, the mosque was destroyed in the night between the 14th and the 15th of March, and the Assembly of Republika Srpska had its session to discuss the Vance-Owen Plan much later than that. And could you please now order the Prosecutor to get the exact -- the correct and accurate data on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you seemed very sure about what you were saying. There seems to be a 24-hour differential here. You said that it was between the 12th and the 13th. Mr. Seselj is saying that it's between the 14th and the 15th. So we don't quite know what the exact date is anymore.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 12th and 13th is what is stated in my entry. It may have been a problem in translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, Mr. Seselj talked about the 14th and the 15th. Maybe there's a mistake, but this is not the point. When I put you the question innocently to understand why everything was clean, you told me that the municipality had intervened, and you provided me with a piece of information. And then you added it was on the next day following the explosion that people were sent in to clean this up. The accused is now telling us that as far as he is concerned, the municipality meetings of Republika Srpska occurred well after that, a long time after that. He might be right, he might be wrong. You might be right, you might be wrong. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. President, as far as I can recall, the Republika Srpska Assembly was in session. The witness said it was the National Assembly of Republika Srpska that was in session, and to my knowledge this happened two months later. So it's not my mistake. Whether it's the 13th or the 14th, that's beside the point. It's the gap, the gap of maybe 24 hours or two days. You could still link it to the session of the Assembly, but the Assembly was in session at a much later date. We've already had this in front of us, and before you prohibited the debate about who perpetrated this, we did have this debate. And now a link is established a session of the Republika Srpska National Assembly, and that's not in the expert report at all. This is something that the expert has just come up with out of the thin air.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The meeting of the Assembly of the Republika Srpska seems to have occurred two months later. You don't seem to agree. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I merely mention, as an explanation for why so many reporters were in town, whether it was that particular meeting to which Mr. Seselj is referring, I have no idea, but I recall that there was a meeting of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, I note for the record that we believe it's improper for the accused to object to answers given by witnesses, but I'll move on. May we have the next slide, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This mosque is described, beginning on page 496 of the Serbian version of the report. In the English, the relevant page begins on ERN number 0469-2745. Mr. Riedlmayer, can you tell us a little bit about what's depicted on the slide that's in front of you at the moment?

Yes. It is reputed to be the second-oldest mosque in Bosnia. It's the mosque of Sultan Mehmed the Conqueror in Kuslat Municipality. It is located south of Zvornik, atop a high cliff overlooking the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: This slide that we see in front of us, can you tell us about what it shows and when this drawing was made?

Okay. The drawing was published in 1984. It is a view of the mosque, and I would call the Court's attention a little bit to the topography, because it will help you understand the next slide. You see the mosque located at the left edge of the precipice of the cliff. The ground underneath the mosque is level. Then between the mosque and the higher outcrop of rock at right, there is some vegetation that's visible down below, and then there is a higher outcropping at the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Next slide, please.

This is a view taken from that higher outcrop down towards the mosque. You can, first of all, see how immensely high up it is, that those are trees down below. It was a traditional Bosnian mosque with stone walls and a wooden roof and a wooden minaret, and metal finial at the top of the minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Go to the next slide, please.

The picture at left comes from Bosnia's Institute for the Protection of Cultural Heritage, and you can see the mosque on top of the cliff. The second picture, the one at the right, was taken in May of 2002 by a Tribunal investigator. I have a picture of my own, but at that time I didn't have the "before" picture, and this shows a better angle, the one -- I was there two months later. Just to orient you as to what is happening, again if you look at the black-and-white image on the left, you can see the level area of the mosque, and then next to the mosque, a patch of vegetation and then the higher outcropping. What is a little bit confusing is that the second picture, the one at the right, is taken from a slightly different angle. First of all, the "before" picture was taken from the next hillside, which is why you see the mountains in the background. The second picture was taken from the bottom of the valley, which makes those mountains disappear. Also, the second picture, the "after" picture, was taken a little bit to the left, which makes the outcropping that the mosque was on look much slimmer, because you're looking at it edge-on. But I think now that you've seen several pictures, you have no problem in identifying where the mosque stood, which is now a little level plot of ground, and then the patch of vegetation and then the higher outcropping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Judges, please do not allow the witness to mislead you in this way. You can see on the next -- on the second photograph that there is no space where the mosque was. It is not there. It's the summit. Well, if the photograph was indeed taken from the same place, you can see the beginning of the summit to the far right of the mosque, and the area where the mosque was does not exist on the second photograph. Please have a look and you will see. I think this is really inappropriate, what the witness is doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the only problem that anyone may have in this courtroom is this: We have two photographs. We have an old photograph, where we see a mosque. We have a second photograph where there is no mosque. So without having been to school, you might well ask, "Where has the mosque gone?" You don't need to have written a PhD to wonder why this is the case. On the second photograph, it looks as if there's no mosque. Is that what you wanted to tell us, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, please allow me to say that there is no space where the mosque was. On the second photograph, there is no space where the mosque was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. Seselj, you can ask all these questions and go into details during the cross-examination, and that way you will not keep interrupting the Prosecutor. It's very difficult for us, also, you know to keep track of things with you and your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, for the record, we reiterate this as a proper ground for cross-examination and or argument and is inappropriate at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Riedlmayer, can you tell us, sir, how does one gain access to this mosque, or how did one gain access to this mosque?

Okay. Your Honour, the main highway is at the bottom of the valley that you see on the photo at right, where the trees are. It is the main highway heading out of Zvornik, and this is the spot where the highway turns away from the river. To go up to the mosque requires a two-hour climb up an unpaved road. It is not an easy place to get to the mosque served the inhabitants of a couple of small villages up on the mountain, I was told. This is actually why I had to rely on a photograph taken from down below, rather than making that climb. I had limited time in Bosnia, and it would have taken an entire day to climb two hours up and two hours down just to take a photograph immediately on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would now like to turn to what could very well be the last topic we reach today. You mentioned earlier, Mr. Riedlmayer, a mosque which had not been destroyed because it was inactive. Do you remember telling us about that, sir?
Yes, in Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
