utterances.text: Other than that mosque, sir, what, if anything, can you tell us about other inactive mosques in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what happened to those inactive mosques during the war?

Okay. In my survey, I found a small number of mosques, three altogether, in the Republika Srpska, three within this survey, although I saw others in other municipalities for other surveys, three mosques that had suffered relatively minor damage in municipalities where every other mosque had been seriously damaged or completely destroyed. And in all cases where mosques in these municipalities had been left only lightly damaged, the mosques were mosques that were under construction on the eve of the war. Under the laws of the former Yugoslavia, religious communities registered these monuments at the time that they went into active use, and so these mosques had not yet been dedicated or registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If we could please then go to the next slide. And again, Mr. Riedlmayer, for the benefit of Dr. Seselj, could you read the caption on the left of this slide, please.
The caption on the left says: "Inactive sites were missed."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And for the benefit of the accused, this mosque that's depicted in this photograph is described in page 426 of the Serbian language version of the annex. The English version may be found at ERN page number 0469-2847. Can you describe, Mr. Riedlmayer, what is shown in this photograph?

What you see in this photograph is the new mosque at the village of Donji Krizevici. Donji Krizevici is a village on the highway heading out of the town of Zvornik to the northwest, just a few kilometres out of town, and I saw the mosque immediately next to the highway. As you can see, the mosque is still under construction. You can see not only the raw brick but also, if you look carefully to the left of the dome, you can see the reinforced -- reinforced steel bars that will support the minaret once it's made. What struck me about it is even though the building is under construction, it is readily recognisable as a mosque. It is also in a very accessible spot, within sight of the highway, and yet it seemed to have escaped the fate of the other mosques in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And perhaps -- perhaps I missed it, Mr. Riedlmayer, but can you tell us, if you know, when this photograph was taken?

Oh, I'm sorry. The photograph was taken in May of 2002 by a Tribunal investigator. You can see the Tribunal registration numbers at the top right. I just thought it was a clearer photograph than the one I took. I also visited the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. If we could please then go to the next slide. Information concerning this mosque may be found on page 604 in the Serbian version. In the English version, at ERN number 0469-2598.

Okay. This is an unfinished mosque in the village of Janjari, which is near Bijeljina, on the border with the neighbouring municipality of Ugljevik, and once again you can see the unfinished minaret at right and you can see the concrete frame and some in-fill brick, some of which appears to be missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how do you know, Mr. Riedlmayer, that this was an unfinished mosque?

Well, some of it is just looking at it in common sense, but I also spoke to an informant from the village, who told me that the mosque had been under construction on the eve of the war and had already been used as an overflow worship space during the last Bajram or Muslim holiday just before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can we go to the next slide, please. And what's depicted in this slide, sir?

This is the same building, again turned 90 degrees. The previous shot was taken from the left. And, once again, you can see that there is -- there are building materials missing from the mosque, but that in spite of the fact that it's next to the highway, nothing worse has happened to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I'm not sure how much time I have left. Perhaps if the Registrar can give me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar told me about five minutes ago that you had used up one hour and thirty-five minutes, so theoretically you have about fifteen minutes left. Witness, please, I have an important question to ask. I'm seeing the photograph of this mosque, which at the time was under construction. If I'm not wrong, this mosque was under construction at the time, and the way it looks now, is it the way it looked in 1992-1993, when the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can only go by what I looked at and put it in the context of what I was told. If you look both at this photo and the previous one, you can see that this is not the way buildings look when they are being systematically constructed. Somebody has opportunistically, I assume, raided it for building materials and removed some elements. I also found graffiti inside, actually within the initials of Mr. Seselj's party, but I had no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wanted to get to this. As a Judge, I'm looking at this photograph, together with my fellow Judges, and we see a building with concrete, reinforced concrete, probably, probably have these metal rods in the concrete. There's also bricks. Obviously, there are some bricks missing, but there's still some bricks left also. In your document, there's the following mention. It says: "This mosque has been vandalised and there are SRS graffitis on it." Now, a simple mind could immediately make a connection and say that vandals destroyed everything, destroyed as much as possible, and that these vandals are members of the Serbian Radical Party. But this graffiti, did you see them with your own eyes or were you told about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your Honour, they were on the interior of the building, where the light wasn't good, so you couldn't take photos of them, but I did see them. On the other hand, I did see this in the summer of 2002. I have no knowledge of when the graffiti appeared on the building. I believe that what is significant about this mosque is not the graffiti, as such, but the fact that it survived relatively undamaged, while finished mosques nearby were destroyed. I think it is simply a fact I felt worth remarking on, especially when you compare it to the previous site I showed at Kuslat, where a mosque that was exceedingly difficult to get to was nevertheless destroyed in the middle of the war, something that would have taken considerable enterprise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This graffiti that you read or saw, what do you attribute it to? You have graffitis everywhere, "US go home," everywhere, I mean a lot of graffitis everywhere, so what meaning did you give to this graffiti?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No actual significance, Your Honour, except for the fact that graffiti of this sort is something I often saw next to the ruins or the sites of destroyed mosques. So at the very least, it indicates that there are people around there who feel these as a focus of hostilities. That's all I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking, I mean, graffitis are on walls, so theoretically we should see graffiti all over the walls, but we don't see any. It's inside that you find the graffiti.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case, yes. In other cases, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I note the time. The Prosecution does have one issue to raise with respect to next week, and I would ask, perhaps with your permission, the witness could be excused until Tuesday, and then my colleague has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you will please come back next week, please, and rest assured, once Mr. Mundis's 20 minutes are up, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Seselj for two hours, and after that you will be allowed home. Don't worry. Unfortunately, you're going to have to spend the weekend in Holland, or maybe you could go and visit some historic sites over here, and that way you will not completely waste your time over the weekend. I will now ask the usher to please escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like a private session, Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I will yield the floor to my colleague, Mr. Marcussen, who will address you and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think we can start in open session, but we will probably have to go into private session at some point, and I'll indicate when. Your Honours, I'm on my feet to make an application for the admission of a written statement of the next witness into evidence, pursuant to Rule 92 ter, so that would be Witness VS-51. Your Honours recall that a number of motions were filed for the admission of written evidence for a lot of witnesses at the pre-trial phase. On the 31st of October, 2007, the Prosecution filed a consolidated motion on the same issue, requesting the admission of statements and transcripts from witnesses into evidence under Rule 92 ter. This request included 33 witnesses whose transcripts from other cases were being requested admitted into evidence, including VS-51. On the 7th of January, the Trial Chamber, in its decision on the Prosecution's consolidated motion pursuant to Rules 89(F), 92 bis, 92 ter and 92 quater of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, ruled on these requests.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 48 and 49 of the decision, the Trial Chamber found that it was in the interests of justice --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down? Could you please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... only transcripts with respect to witnesses who were not either insiders or who would give evidence about matters on which the Trial Chamber ultimately had to rule, but it was closely related to the indictment. On this basis, the Trial Chamber specifically denied the admission on the 92 ter of two witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please slow down. You're speaking much too fast, you're reading much too fast. The interpreters are completely lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I will go back. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Read slowly, read slowly. The interpreters do not have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... under 92 -- sorry. In your 7th January 2008 decision, Your Honours applied an "interest of justice" test, which essentially was -- where you found that it was not in the interests of justice to admit transcripts of witnesses that were so-called "insiders" and transcripts which were closely related to the indictment and therefore went directly to issues upon which the Trial Chamber had to rule. There were two witnesses who were found to be in that category, VS-04 and Milan Babic, and the request for the admission of evidence -- for the request of transcripts of those two witnesses were dismissed on the basis that it would not be in the interests of justice to admit those transcripts. The remaining 31 witnesses, with respect to those witnesses, the Trial Chamber noted that more than 8.000 pages of material had been put forward by the Prosecution and that the Prosecution had failed to establish the relevance of the material. Among those 31 witnesses were VS-51. So the Trial Chamber dismissed the request for the admission of the transcripts of these witnesses, but invited or indicated to the Prosecution that the Prosecution could file new statements that were tailored specifically to this case, and the Trial Chamber would consider the admission of such statements pursuant to Rule 92 ter. So it's my understanding that the Trial Chamber found that it could be in the interests of justice to admit written evidence from these 31 witnesses, including VS-51, provided that the Prosecution come with a focused statement and establish the relevance of the evidence. The Prosecution is preparing a new statement from this witness, from VS-51. It is based largely on a statement that the witness gave earlier to the Prosecution in 2002, with the addition of some material we consolidate in from some additional information he provided in 2006 and maybe a few bits from his prior testimony, with a view to have one consolidated document that contains the evidence of VS-51. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me stop you here to save time, because I'm looking at the clock and I will be sitting on another hearing in just an hour. So in this decision, we said that if you did this, you were supposed to provide this to us 14 days before the witness actually came. VS-51 is scheduled for next week, so you did not meet this 14-day criteria. So that now being said, there will not be a 92 ter for VS-51.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course, if that's your decision already at this stage, then we would -- I would note we have had, of course, considerable difficulties, as Your Honours know, having contact with this particular witness and have therefore not had an opportunity to prepare a statement, but we can do him as a live witness. Obviously, we're prepared to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, viva voce, and I will tell you how long you will be granted for this. But next week, we still have this witness to finish. Tuesday will probably be used up by Mr. Riedlmayer. We will start with 51, but we probably won't finish 51 by Thursday, so you will have to tell him that he has to do what is necessary to spend an additional weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... which were also part of the reasons we put forward the request. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's time to end, it's time to finish. Just a few seconds for Mr. Seselj and then we'll put an end to this hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that the Witness VS-51 is one of the most important witnesses in this trial. You will remember that the thesis of my defence, my defence case, is that General Aleksandar Vasiljevic organised the execution of the prisoners of war in Ovcara and -- well, I don't need to go on. He was the perpetrator --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you no longer have the floor to speak about this. Witness VS-51 will come and we will see. Let's no anticipate on whatever will happen with this witness. The Prosecution is calling him and we will see what will happen. You are -- what you just said should be in cross-examination. Furthermore, I want to repeat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything stopped now, the machine stopped. I think it works now. So let me just tell to the Prosecution that housekeeping matters must be raised early in the hearing, when we start, because when you raise a housekeeping matter or a procedural matter at the very end of the hearing, systematically Mr. Seselj wants the floor to reply, we end up not -- going overtime. So administrative matters must absolutely be dealt with at the beginning of the hearing and not at the end. Secondly, regarding Witness VS-51, it will be a viva voce witness. Therefore, there's no problems for the procedure to come. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of May, 2008, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.20 p.m.,
